topics.t: Why a society needs basic rules
topics.h: Imagine a hostel of 500 students with no agreed rules: who decides lights-out, who settles fights, who controls the mess money? Within a week, nobody trusts anybody. A constitution solves exactly this problem for a whole country.
p: A constitution is a set of basic rules that allows minimal coordination and trust among members of a society.
Coordination and assurance: everyone knows the minimum rules that others will also follow, so people can plan and cooperate without fear.
First function: it specifies the basic allocation of power, i.e. who has the power to make decisions and how the government is constituted.
In India, the Constitution says Parliament makes laws and that Parliament itself is organised in a particular way (two Houses, elected members, procedures).
Thought experiment: in a society without agreed rules, every decision would be disputed and the strongest would simply impose their will.

ex.q: A group of 30 villagers must decide how to share water from a new tubewell. They first agree that a five-member committee, elected every year, will fix the timetable. Which function of a constitution does this first agreement perform?
st: Ask: does the agreement settle a specific water timetable, or who will decide it?
It settles who has the authority to decide (the elected committee) and how that body is formed.
Deciding who decides is the allocation of decision-making power.
ex.a: It specifies who has the power to make decisions — the first function of a constitution.

topics.rl: Every cricket tournament, from gully cricket to the IPL, starts with agreed basic rules: who is the umpire, whose decision is final, how disputes go to the third umpire. A constitution does the same for the nation.

topics.h: Even a government elected by crores of voters cannot ban you from speaking your mind or practising your religion. Why? Because the Constitution draws lines that no government may cross.
p: Second function: a constitution sets limits on what a government can impose on citizens. These limits are fundamental, so government may never trespass them.
Limits usually take the form of fundamental rights, e.g. freedom of speech, freedom of association, and protection against arbitrary arrest.

Third function: it enables the government to fulfil the aspirations of a society and create conditions for a just society, e.g. the Indian Constitution empowers the state to end caste discrimination and reduce inequality.
Fourth function: it expresses the fundamental identity of a people. Through it, people agree on basic norms and become a political community.

Constitutions differ in how they balance national identity with other identities like religion, region or language; the Indian Constitution does not tie national identity to any single religion or language.

ex.q: Identify the function served by: (i) Article 17 abolishing untouchability, (ii) the right to freedom of speech, (iii) the Preamble beginning 'We, the people of India'.
st: (i) Ending untouchability works to change society, so it enables the state to fulfil aspirations of justice.
(ii) Free speech is a limit the state cannot cross: it limits government power.
(iii) The Preamble declares who 'we' are as one political community: it expresses identity.
ex.a: (i) Fulfils aspirations of a just society; (ii) limits government power; (iii) expresses the identity of the people.

topics.rl: When the Supreme Court strikes down a law that curbs free speech, it is enforcing the 'limits' function. When Parliament passes a law like the Right to Education Act, it is using the 'enabling' function.

topics.t: Where a constitution gets its authority
topics.h: Many countries have had beautiful-sounding constitutions that were thrown away within a few years. India's has lasted since 1950. What makes some constitutions command respect while others die on paper?
p: 'Constitution' can mean a single written document, or the whole working body of rules by which a country is governed. Most countries have a written document; some, like the United Kingdom, have no single document.

Mode of promulgation: a constitution has more authority when it is drafted by people with popular credibility (like a Constituent Assembly of national leaders) rather than imposed by a military ruler or an unpopular leader.
Substantive provisions: people will accept a constitution if its basic rules give everyone some reason to go along with it, e.g. by protecting freedom and equality.

Balanced institutional design: power is divided among institutions with checks so no single group can subvert the constitution; it should be neither too rigid nor too flexible, protecting core values while allowing amendment.
Constitutions that lacked these qualities have often been suspended or set aside, e.g. Pakistan's 1956 constitution was abrogated in 1958.

ex.q: Why does the Indian Constitution enjoy strong authority? Give three reasons.
st: Promulgation: it was drafted by a Constituent Assembly of leaders who had wide public credibility from the national movement.
Substance: it protects rights and equal citizenship, giving every group a reason to accept it.
Design: power is divided among legislature, executive, judiciary and independent bodies, and the Constitution can be amended without losing its core values.
ex.a: Credible mode of promulgation, fair substantive provisions, and balanced institutional design.

topics.rl: Think of the ICC rule book: players accept it because it was drafted by representatives of all cricket boards, treats every team equally, and lets the third umpire check the on-field umpire. Credibility, fairness and checks — the same three sources of a constitution's authority.

topics.t: The Constituent Assembly: who and when
topics.h: In December 1946 a few hundred men and women met in New Delhi to write the rulebook for over 30 crore people. Who chose them, and how did they speak for such a diverse land?
p: The Constituent Assembly first met on 9 December 1946 and re-assembled as the Constituent Assembly for divided India on 14 August 1947.
Its members were elected indirectly, by members of the provincial legislative assemblies, under the scheme proposed by the Cabinet Mission (1946).
Seats were allotted roughly in proportion to population, about one seat for every 10 lakh (one million) people. Provinces elected their members; princely states were also given seats.
Within each province, seats were divided among three communities — Muslims, Sikhs and General — and each community's members in the provincial assembly elected its representatives.

The Congress dominated the Assembly, but it contained a wide range of opinions and groups. The Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949 and came into force on 26 January 1950, after about 2 years 11 months of work.

ex.q: Arrange the key dates of the Constituent Assembly and explain why 26 January was chosen.
st: 9 December 1946: first meeting of the Assembly.
14 August 1947: re-assembles as the Assembly for divided India.
26 November 1949: Constitution adopted.
26 January 1950: Constitution comes into force — the date recalls 26 January 1930, when the Congress celebrated Purna Swaraj Day.
ex.a: 1946 → 1947 → adopted 26 Nov 1949 → in force 26 Jan 1950.

topics.rl: Every 26 November India celebrates Constitution Day (Samvidhan Divas), and 26 January is Republic Day, with the parade on Kartavya Path. One date marks adoption, the other marks commencement.

topics.t: How the Assembly worked: procedure and inheritance
topics.h: The Constituent Assembly debates fill thousands of printed pages. Members argued for hours over a single clause. Why did they take such pains instead of simply voting things through?
p: Procedure: the Assembly worked through open public discussion and reasoned deliberation, seeking consensus rather than imposing the will of the majority.

It had eight major committees, usually chaired by leaders such as Jawaharlal Nehru, Rajendra Prasad, Sardar Patel, Maulana Azad or B.R. Ambedkar. The Drafting Committee was chaired by Dr B.R. Ambedkar.
Inheritance of the nationalist movement: the Motilal Nehru Report (1928) and the Karachi Resolution of the Congress (1931) had already demanded rights and a democratic constitution.

The Objectives Resolution, moved by Jawaharlal Nehru in December 1946, set out the Assembly's guiding aims: an independent sovereign republic, all power derived from the people, justice, equality and freedom for all, and safeguards for minorities and backward and tribal areas.

Institutional arrangements were balanced among legislature, executive, judiciary and Centre and states. Many administrative details drew on the Government of India Act 1935, while the whole framework embodies democratic values as a living framework.

ex.q: Show how the Objectives Resolution's ideas appear in the final Constitution.
st: 'Sovereign republic' → India is a Sovereign Democratic Republic (Preamble).
'All power derived from the people' → Preamble begins 'We, the people of India'.
'Justice, equality, freedom' → Preamble's justice, liberty, equality; Fundamental Rights.
'Safeguards for minorities, backward and tribal areas' → cultural and educational rights, reservations, special provisions.
ex.a: The Objectives Resolution's principles became the Preamble and key provisions of the Constitution.

topics.rl: Committee meetings in today's Parliament, where members from different parties study a bill clause by clause, carry forward the Assembly's habit of patient deliberation.

topics.h: Critics once called the Indian Constitution a 'bag of borrowings'. But a great chef borrowing spices from many kitchens still cooks a dish that is entirely their own.
p: British Constitution: first-past-the-post, parliamentary form of government, the idea of the rule of law, the institution of the Speaker and its role, and the law-making procedure.
United States Constitution: a charter of fundamental rights, the power of judicial review and the independence of the judiciary.
Irish Constitution: the Directive Principles of State Policy.

French Constitution: the principles of liberty, equality and fraternity. Canadian Constitution: a quasi-federal form of government (a federal system with a strong central government) and the idea of residual powers with the Centre.
The makers did not copy blindly: they examined each idea and adapted it to Indian conditions and to the ideals of the national movement.

ex.q: A student says: 'Judicial review and the Speaker both came from Britain.' Correct the statement.
st: The Speaker, parliamentary government, rule of law and FPTP came from Britain.
Judicial review, a charter of fundamental rights and independence of the judiciary came from the USA.
So only the Speaker is British; judicial review is American.
ex.a: Speaker → Britain; judicial review → USA.

topics.rl: Like ISRO adapting ideas from around the world into frugal Indian missions such as Chandrayaan, the makers adapted foreign ideas into a uniquely Indian design.

topics.ch: Constitution: Rights in the Indian Constitution
topics.t: Why rights matter: the Bill of Rights
topics.h: If the police could lock you up without reason or a minister could shut your newspaper on a whim, would any promise of democracy mean anything? Rights are the guarantees that make democracy real.
p: Rights are guarantees that protect individuals against the state and against other individuals and groups, so that no one can trample on their dignity and freedom.
A Bill of Rights is a list of rights written into a constitution; it marks what the government cannot do and ensures remedies if rights are violated.
A remedy matters as much as the right itself: rights in the Indian Constitution can be enforced in the courts.
Demands for rights grew in the freedom struggle, e.g. the Motilal Nehru Report (1928) called for a bill of rights; these were placed in Part III as Fundamental Rights.

Fundamental Rights differ from ordinary legal rights: a legal right can be changed by an ordinary law, but a Fundamental Right can be changed only by amending the Constitution. Fundamental Rights are not absolute; the state may impose reasonable restrictions.

ex.q: A State law reduces the minimum wage set by an earlier State law. Another law tries to take away freedom of speech completely. Which can be done by ordinary law-making?
st: The minimum wage is a legal right created by ordinary law, so ordinary law can change it.
Freedom of speech is a Fundamental Right in Part III; it cannot be taken away by ordinary law.
Only reasonable restrictions on speech are allowed, and any change to the right itself needs a constitutional amendment (which courts can review).
ex.a: Changing the minimum wage is possible by ordinary law; abolishing free speech is not.

topics.rl: When a citizen petitions a High Court after being denied a ration card on discriminatory grounds, the Bill of Rights becomes a working tool, not just words.

topics.ch: Constitution: Rights in the Indian Constitution
topics.h: A minister's son and a rickshaw puller's daughter stand before the same court and the same law. That simple idea took centuries to win.
p: Article 14: equality before the law and equal protection of the laws for all persons within India.

Article 15: no discrimination by the state on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth; equal access to shops, restaurants, wells, public places. The state may make special provisions for women, children and socially and educationally backward classes, SC and ST.
Article 16: equality of opportunity in public employment; reservation for backward classes is allowed.
Article 17: untouchability is abolished and its practice in any form is forbidden and punishable.
Article 18: titles (other than military or academic distinctions) are abolished, so no citizen gets a hereditary rank.

ex.q: A restaurant owner refuses to serve a customer because of his caste. Which Article is violated, and why?
st: The customer is denied access to a place of public entertainment on grounds of caste.
Article 15 forbids such discrimination in access to shops, restaurants and public places.
If the refusal is based on 'untouchability' practices, Article 17 is also violated.
ex.a: Article 15 (and Article 17 if it is untouchability).

topics.rl: Women-only coaches in Indian Railways and reserved seats for women in buses show Article 15's permission for special provisions for women; they do not violate equality.

topics.ch: Constitution: Rights in the Indian Constitution
topics.t: Right to Freedom: Article 19 and Article 21
topics.h: A street vendor in Mumbai, a journalist in Kolkata and a student who moves from Bihar to Bengaluru all use freedoms written into Article 19 every single day.
p: Article 19 gives all citizens six freedoms: speech and expression; to assemble peacefully without arms; to form associations and unions; to move freely throughout India; to reside and settle in any part of India; to practise any profession or carry on any occupation, trade or business.
Each freedom is subject to reasonable restrictions, e.g. for the sovereignty and integrity of India, security of the state, public order, decency or morality.
Article 21: no person shall be deprived of life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law. It is the most fundamental of all rights.

The Supreme Court has expanded Article 21: right to life includes a life with dignity, the right to shelter and livelihood, and the right to education (now Article 21A for children aged 6 to 14, added by the 86th Amendment in 2002).
The freedom to own property was earlier listed in Article 19 but was removed; today Article 19 has six freedoms.

ex.q: Pavement dwellers in a city face eviction without any rehabilitation. They argue that losing their shelter means losing their livelihood. Which right supports them?
st: Their claim is about survival and livelihood, not just property.
The Supreme Court has held that the right to life (Article 21) includes the right to livelihood.
So the state must follow a fair procedure before eviction.
ex.a: Article 21, as interpreted to include the right to livelihood and shelter.

topics.rl: A student moving from Patna to Pune for college and later starting a food truck uses the freedoms to move, reside and carry on business — Article 19(1)(d), (e) and (g).

topics.ch: Constitution: Rights in the Indian Constitution
topics.t: Rights of the accused and preventive detention
topics.h: In many countries people vanish into jails for years without being told why. The Indian Constitution has clear rules to stop that — even for people accused of crimes.
p: Article 22: a person who is arrested must be told the grounds of arrest, has the right to consult and be defended by a lawyer, and must be produced before the nearest magistrate within 24 hours (excluding travel time).

Article 20: no one can be punished for an act that was not an offence when committed; no one can be prosecuted and punished more than once for the same offence (no double jeopardy); no one can be compelled to be a witness against himself (no self-incrimination).
Preventive detention: a person may be detained to prevent a feared future act that threatens law and order or national security, even before any offence is committed.
Safeguards: detention is for a limited period, and longer detention needs review by an advisory board; the detained person must be told the grounds and can make a representation.
Criticism: preventive detention laws can be misused against political opponents or to silence dissent, so they are debated as a balance between security and liberty.

ex.q: Ravi is arrested at 10 a.m. on Monday. The nearest magistrate's court is two hours away. By when must he be produced, and what else must happen?
st: The limit is 24 hours from arrest, excluding the time taken for the journey to the court.
So he must be produced by about 10 a.m. Tuesday plus the 2-hour journey time, i.e. by about 12 noon Tuesday.
He must also be told the grounds of arrest and allowed to consult a lawyer.
ex.a: Within 24 hours plus travel time (by about noon Tuesday), after being told the grounds and allowed a lawyer.

topics.rl: Police stations across India display 'D.K. Basu guidelines' on arrest, which build on Article 22: an arrest memo, informing a relative, and medical examination.

topics.ch: Constitution: Rights in the Indian Constitution
topics.h: A 12-year-old working in a firecracker factory, a family forced into unpaid labour to repay a debt — the Constitution names these practices and bans them outright.
p: Right against Exploitation (Articles 23–24): bans traffic in human beings, 'begar' (forced labour without payment) and other forced labour; bans employment of children below 14 years in factories, mines and other hazardous work.

Freedom of Religion (Articles 25–28): freedom of conscience and the right to profess, practise and propagate religion, subject to public order, morality and health. The state can regulate secular activities linked to religion and make social reforms.

Every religious group may manage its own religious affairs; no one can be compelled to pay taxes for the promotion of a particular religion; no religious instruction in institutions wholly maintained by state funds.
India is a secular state: it has no official religion and treats all religions with equal respect, giving individuals freedom to practise any religion or none.

Cultural and Educational Rights (Articles 29–30): any section of citizens with a distinct language, script or culture may conserve it; minorities, religious or linguistic, may establish and administer educational institutions of their choice.

ex.q: A linguistic minority group wants to set up a school that teaches in its own language. Which right supports them?
st: The group is a linguistic minority.
Article 30 lets religious or linguistic minorities establish and administer educational institutions of their choice.
Article 29 also protects their right to conserve their distinct language and script.
ex.a: Cultural and Educational Rights — Articles 29 and 30.

topics.rl: Child-rescue operations by labour departments in cities like Delhi and Hyderabad, freeing children from hazardous workshops, enforce Article 24.

topics.ch: Constitution: Rights in the Indian Constitution
topics.t: Constitutional remedies, writs and the NHRC
topics.h: Dr Ambedkar called one right 'the very soul of the Constitution and the very heart of it'. Without it, every other right would be a promise without a guarantee.
p: Right to Constitutional Remedies (Article 32): a citizen can move the Supreme Court directly for enforcement of Fundamental Rights; High Courts have similar powers under Article 226. Ambedkar called it the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution.

Habeas corpus: the court orders that an arrested person be produced before it; it can free a person detained unlawfully. Mandamus: an order to a public official to perform a legal duty they are not doing.

Prohibition: a higher court orders a lower court to stop proceedings in a case beyond its jurisdiction. Certiorari: a higher court transfers a case from a lower court or authority to itself, or quashes its order.
Quo warranto: the court asks 'by what authority' a person holds an office, and can stop someone holding it without being entitled.

The National Human Rights Commission (set up in 1993) inquires into complaints of human rights violations and makes recommendations; it cannot punish the guilty itself. The Right to Property was removed from Fundamental Rights by the 44th Amendment (1978) and is now a constitutional/legal right.

ex.q: Match each situation to a writ: (a) a person is held by police with no reason given; (b) a municipal officer refuses to issue a licence the law requires him to issue; (c) a person who is not qualified occupies a public office.
st: (a) Unlawful detention → produce the body → habeas corpus.
(b) Official not performing a legal duty → mandamus ('we command').
(c) Holding office without authority → quo warranto.
ex.a: (a) Habeas corpus, (b) mandamus, (c) quo warranto.

topics.rl: When the family of a missing person files a habeas corpus petition in a High Court, judges can order the police to produce that person in court within days.

topics.ch: Constitution: Rights in the Indian Constitution
topics.h: Free school education, panchayats in every village, guaranteed wage work for rural households — many of India's big welfare laws began life as 'directives' that no court could enforce.
p: Directive Principles of State Policy (Part IV) are guidelines to the state for building a just society. They are non-justiciable: courts cannot enforce them, but they are fundamental in the governance of the country.
Goals: welfare of the people; social, economic and political justice; raising the standard of living; equitable distribution of resources; promotion of international peace.
Policies: a uniform civil code; prohibition of consumption of alcoholic liquor; promotion of cottage industries; prevention of slaughter of useful cattle; promotion of village panchayats.

Non-justiciable rights (desired, not enforceable): adequate means of livelihood; equal pay for equal work for men and women; right against economic exploitation; right to work; early childhood care and education for children below six years.

Many DPSPs were later implemented by laws, e.g. panchayats (73rd Amendment), the Right to Education Act, and the rural employment guarantee law (MGNREGA, 2005, which Parliament replaced in 2025 with a new rural jobs guarantee law, the VB-G RAM G Act).

ex.q: A woman worker in a factory is paid less than a man for the same work. Can she go to court under the Directive Principles? What else can she use?
st: 'Equal pay for equal work for both men and women' is a Directive Principle.
DPSPs are non-justiciable, so she cannot enforce the DPSP itself in court.
But Parliament has passed laws on equal remuneration, and she can enforce those laws.
ex.a: Not under the DPSP directly, but under the law Parliament passed to implement it.

topics.rl: MGNREGA (2005) gave every rural household a legal guarantee of wage employment, turning the DPSP 'right to work' into a legal entitlement. In 2025 Parliament replaced it with a new rural employment guarantee law (the VB-G RAM G Act), but the idea is the same: a Directive Principle made into an enforceable law.

topics.ch: Constitution: Rights in the Indian Constitution
topics.t: Fundamental Duties and FR versus DPSP
topics.h: The right to property versus land for the landless: in the 1950s this clash between a Fundamental Right and a Directive Principle sparked India's biggest constitutional battles.
p: Fundamental Duties (Article 51A, Part IVA) were added by the 42nd Amendment (1976). Ten duties were listed originally; an eleventh (parents to provide education to children aged 6–14) was added in 2002. They are not enforceable by courts.

Examples of duties: abide by the Constitution and respect the National Flag and Anthem; defend the country; promote harmony; protect the natural environment; develop scientific temper; safeguard public property.
Fundamental Rights mainly protect individuals and restrain the state; Directive Principles direct the state to act positively. Rights are justiciable; DPSPs are not.

Conflict: the right to property clashed with DPSP-based land reforms and abolition of zamindari. Parliament passed amendments to protect land reform laws; the right to property was finally removed from Part III in 1978.
The courts have since held that FR and DPSP complement each other: harmony and balance between them is part of the Constitution's basic design.

ex.q: A State law takes surplus land from big landlords to distribute to the landless. A landlord says his Fundamental Right to property is violated. Explain the clash.
st: The law implements DPSP goals of preventing concentration of wealth and promoting justice.
In the 1950s–70s, the right to property was a Fundamental Right, so landlords challenged such laws.
Parliament amended the Constitution to protect land reforms, and in 1978 property ceased to be a Fundamental Right.
ex.a: It is a classic FR (property) vs DPSP (equitable distribution) conflict, resolved in favour of reform.

topics.rl: School campaigns on Swachh Bharat, tree-planting drives and not damaging railway property all reflect Fundamental Duties such as protecting the environment and safeguarding public property.

topics.h: Over 96 crore Indians were registered voters for the 2024 Lok Sabha election. Imagine all of them trying to debate every budget clause together in one giant meeting!
p: Direct democracy: citizens themselves take part in day-to-day decision-making, as in a Gram Sabha or in the small city-states of ancient Greece.
Indirect (representative) democracy: citizens elect representatives who make decisions and run the government on their behalf.
In large modern societies direct democracy is impractical, so elections become the main way people choose who governs and hold them accountable.
Elections must be free and fair; the Constitution therefore lays down the rules: who can vote, who can contest, who supervises elections, and how votes are counted and representatives elected.
Because these rules are in the Constitution (not left to the ruling party), the process is protected from being changed to suit whoever is in power.

ex.q: Classify: (a) all adult villagers meeting to approve the panchayat budget; (b) citizens electing an MP who votes on laws in Parliament.
st: (a) People decide directly in their own meeting → direct democracy.
(b) People choose a representative who decides for them → indirect/representative democracy.
ex.a: (a) Direct democracy; (b) representative democracy.

topics.rl: A Gram Sabha meeting where every adult of the village discusses a new well is a living example of direct democracy inside India's representative system.

topics.h: In a cricket-mad constituency, a candidate can win with just 35% of the votes — while 65% voted for someone else. That's the strange, simple logic of First Past the Post.
p: First Past the Post (FPTP): the country is divided into single-member territorial constituencies; the candidate with more votes than any other wins, even without a majority (plurality system).
Voters vote for a candidate, not just a party; the winner takes all, and votes for losing candidates do not get any seat.
FPTP can give a party many more seats than its vote share: in 1984 the Congress won less than half the votes but more than three-fourths of the Lok Sabha seats.

Why India chose FPTP: it is simple for voters (many of whom were voting for the first time), gives a clear choice of candidate and accountability to a constituency, and tends to produce stable governments in a parliamentary system.
FPTP encourages parties to build broad social coalitions within themselves, since a narrow group rarely wins a seat alone; competition often settles into two main parties or alliances.

ex.q: In a constituency, A gets 38,000 votes, B gets 34,000, C gets 28,000. Who wins under FPTP, and does the winner have a majority?
st: A has the most votes, so A wins.
A's share = 38,000 / 1,00,000 = 38%, which is less than 50%.
ex.a: A wins with 38% — a plurality, not a majority.

topics.rl: India uses FPTP for Lok Sabha and Vidhan Sabha elections, so a single vote can decide a seat: some assembly seats have been won by margins of just a handful of votes.

topics.h: If a party wins 25% of the votes, shouldn't it get 25% of the seats? Countries like Israel and the Netherlands think so — and use a very different system from India's Lok Sabha.
p: Proportional Representation (PR): each party gets seats in proportion to its share of votes. Constituencies are large; the whole country may be one constituency, and several representatives are elected from each.

List system: voters vote for a party; each party publishes a ranked list of candidates, and seats are filled from the list in order. In Israel and the Netherlands the whole country is a single constituency.
In India, PR in the form of the Single Transferable Vote (STV) is used for indirect elections: the President, Vice-President, Rajya Sabha and State Legislative Councils.
STV for Rajya Sabha: MLAs rank candidates in order of preference. Quota to win = (total votes polled ÷ (number of seats + 1)) + 1. Surplus and eliminated votes are transferred by preference.

Comparison: FPTP — small single-member constituencies, vote for a candidate, seats can exceed vote share, often stable majorities; PR — large multi-member constituencies, vote for a party, seats match vote share, often coalitions.

ex.q: Rajasthan's 200 MLAs elect 4 Rajya Sabha members. What is the quota a candidate needs?
st: Quota = (Total votes ÷ (seats + 1)) + 1.
ex.a: 41 first-preference (or transferred) votes.

topics.rl: When you hear that a Rajya Sabha seat was won after counting 'second preferences', that's STV at work in State Assemblies.

topics.h: In a reserved constituency, a Dalit candidate might win with the votes of people from every community. That's exactly what the makers intended — representation without separate electorates.
p: Reserved constituencies: some Lok Sabha and Assembly seats are reserved for Scheduled Castes (SC) and Scheduled Tribes (ST), so these groups get fair representation.

Only candidates from the SC (or ST) community can contest a reserved seat, but ALL voters of the constituency, from every community, vote. This is different from a separate electorate, where only members of a group vote.
The Delimitation Commission, appointed by the President and working with the Election Commission, draws constituency boundaries and decides which seats are reserved, based on the population of SC/ST.
Seats reserved for ST are those with a higher share of ST population; SC-reserved seats take into account both share and spread across regions, and reserved seats can rotate after delimitation.

Women's reservation: after long debate, the Constitution (106th Amendment) Act, 2023 provides for one-third of seats in the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies to be reserved for women, to take effect after the next census and delimitation.

ex.q: In a reserved SC constituency with 15% SC voters, who can contest and who can vote?
st: Contesting: only candidates belonging to the Scheduled Castes.
Voting: every registered voter of the constituency, whatever their community.
So the winner must win support across communities, not only among SC voters.
ex.a: Only SC candidates contest; all voters vote.

topics.rl: When an ST-reserved seat in Jharkhand or Chhattisgarh elects its MLA, voters from all communities living there take part — showing joint electorates in action.

topics.t: Universal franchise and the Election Commission
topics.h: In 1951–52, when many old democracies were still debating who 'deserved' the vote, India gave it to every adult — rich or poor, literate or not, woman or man — in one stroke.
p: Universal adult franchise: every citizen aged 18 or above can vote, regardless of caste, religion, sex, education or wealth. The voting age was lowered from 21 to 18 by the 61st Amendment (1988), first applied in 1989.

Right to contest: a candidate for the Lok Sabha or a State Assembly must be at least 25 years old (30 for Rajya Sabha). There is no educational qualification; certain criminal convictions can disqualify.

Article 324 sets up an independent Election Commission with the 'superintendence, direction and control' of elections to Parliament, State Legislatures, and the offices of President and Vice-President.
The Election Commission is headed by the Chief Election Commissioner (CEC). It was a one-member body until 1989; briefly multi-member in 1989–90, it has been a three-member body since 1993.

Security of tenure: the CEC can be removed only in the same way as a Supreme Court judge, by a special majority of both Houses; other Election Commissioners can be removed only on the CEC's recommendation.

ex.q: Asha is 18, Bhuvan is 24 and Charu is 29. Who can vote, and who can contest for the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha?
st: Voting needs age 18: all three can vote.
Lok Sabha needs age 25: only Charu (29) can contest.
Rajya Sabha needs age 30: none of them yet.
ex.a: All can vote; only Charu can contest the Lok Sabha; none can contest the Rajya Sabha.

topics.rl: When the ECI sets up a polling booth for a single voter deep in a forest or high in the Himalayas, it shows how seriously universal franchise is taken.

topics.h: For about six weeks every five years, the Election Commission becomes one of the most powerful bodies in India: it can transfer officers, order re-polls and rein in the biggest leaders.
p: The EC supervises preparation of an up-to-date voters' list, decides the election schedule, and announces dates for nominations, polling and counting.
It enforces the Model Code of Conduct for parties and candidates, can order a re-poll in a booth or constituency if polling was unfair, and can countermand an election.
It recognises political parties (national or state) and allots election symbols.
During elections, government officers on election duty work under the control of the EC rather than the government.

State Election Commissions (separate from the ECI) conduct elections to panchayats and municipalities. Electronic Voting Machines (EVMs) have been used in all constituencies since the 2004 Lok Sabha election, and turnout has broadly risen over the decades.

ex.q: During polling, there are credible reports of booth capturing at Booth No. 112. What can the Election Commission do?
st: Booth capturing makes the poll at that booth unfair.
The EC can cancel the poll at that booth.
It can then order a re-poll there.
ex.a: Order a re-poll at that booth.

topics.rl: Before every general election the EC launches SVEEP campaigns, with celebrities and cricketers urging first-time voters to enrol and vote.

topics.h: Money power, muscle power, caste appeals, and too few women in Parliament — every democracy has election problems. What reforms have been proposed for India's?
p: Change of system: some suggest shifting from FPTP to a PR or mixed system (like Germany's), so seats better reflect votes.
Women: reserving one-third of seats in Parliament and Assemblies for women (now provided by the 2023 amendment, effective after delimitation).
Money power: stricter limits on and disclosure of election spending; state funding of elections has also been suggested.

Criminalisation: candidates must disclose criminal cases, assets and educational qualifications in affidavits (following Supreme Court directions); proposals to bar candidates facing serious criminal charges.
Caste and religion: a complete ban on appeals to caste and religion in campaigns, and a law to regulate the internal functioning of political parties.

ex.q: Match the problem with the reform: (1) candidates hiding past criminal cases; (2) huge spending by wealthy candidates; (3) seats not matching votes.
st: (1) Mandatory disclosure of criminal record and assets via affidavit.
(2) Strict limits and transparency on spending, or state funding.
(3) Shift towards PR or a mixed system.
ex.a: (1) Disclosure; (2) money controls/state funding; (3) PR or mixed system.

topics.rl: Before you vote, you can check every candidate's affidavit — assets, cases, education — on the ECI's website or app. That disclosure rule is an electoral reform in your pocket.

topics.h: Parliament passes a law guaranteeing rural jobs. But who actually opens the worksites, pays the wages and checks the muster rolls? That's the executive.
p: The executive is the organ of government that implements laws and policies and runs the day-to-day administration.

Political executive: elected leaders (PM, ministers, Chief Ministers) who make policy and change with elections. Permanent executive: civil servants who carry out policy and stay in office regardless of elections.
Presidential system: the President is head of both state and government, usually directly elected, and not responsible to the legislature for survival (e.g. USA, Brazil, most of Latin America).

Parliamentary system: the Prime Minister and cabinet are the real executive and are responsible to the legislature; the head of state (a President or monarch) is mostly nominal (e.g. UK, India, Germany, Italy, Japan, Portugal).

Semi-presidential system: a powerful President and a Prime Minister with a council of ministers share power; the President may belong to a different party from the PM (e.g. France, Russia, Sri Lanka).

ex.q: Classify the executive: (a) a head of state and government directly elected for a fixed term who chooses ministers from outside the legislature; (b) a PM who stays in office only while the lower house supports her; (c) a directly elected President who appoints a PM responsible to parliament.
st: (a) Head of state = head of government, not dependent on legislature → presidential.
(b) Real executive depends on legislature's confidence → parliamentary.
(c) Strong President plus a PM answerable to parliament → semi-presidential.
ex.a: (a) Presidential, (b) parliamentary, (c) semi-presidential.

topics.rl: When a new government takes office after the Lok Sabha elections, ministers change but the District Collector keeps running the district — political executive changes, permanent executive stays.

topics.h: The President of India is the Supreme Commander of the armed forces, signs every law and appoints the Prime Minister — yet is called a 'nominal' head. How can both be true?
p: The Constitution makers chose the parliamentary system because India had experience of it under British rule, it keeps the executive accountable to elected representatives, and it avoids a personality cult around a single all-powerful leader.
The President is the formal head of the state; real executive power is exercised by the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister.
The President is elected indirectly by an electoral college of elected MPs (both Houses) and elected MLAs of the States, using the Single Transferable Vote. A candidate must be at least 35.
Term: five years. The President can be removed only by impeachment for 'violation of the Constitution', which needs a resolution passed by two-thirds of the total membership of each House.
Because the President is not directly elected, no President can claim a personal popular mandate against the elected government.

ex.q: Why might the makers have avoided a directly elected President for India?
st: A directly elected President could claim a popular mandate equal to or greater than the PM's.
This could create two rival centres of power.
An indirectly elected, nominal President keeps real power with the ministry responsible to the Lok Sabha.
ex.a: To avoid rival power centres and keep power with the accountable ministry.

topics.rl: On Republic Day, the President takes the salute at Kartavya Path as Supreme Commander, but the decision to deploy troops is taken by the Union Cabinet — nominal head, real executive.

topics.h: In 1986 a President simply sat on a bill and never signed it. No deadline in the Constitution forced him to act. Welcome to the 'pocket veto'.
p: Formal powers: executive (all executive actions in the President's name), legislative (summoning Parliament, assent to bills), financial (money bills introduced on recommendation), military (Supreme Commander) and diplomatic (treaties, ambassadors). All are exercised on ministers' advice.

Article 74(1): the President shall act in accordance with the advice of the Council of Ministers; the President may ask the Council to reconsider its advice once, but must act on the advice given after reconsideration.
Discretion 1: the right to be informed of all important matters and decisions of the Council of Ministers; the PM must communicate them.

Discretion 2: the President can return a bill (other than a money bill) for reconsideration; if Parliament passes it again, the President must sign. Since no time limit is fixed, the President can keep a bill pending indefinitely — a 'pocket veto', as with the Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill in 1986.
Discretion 3: choosing the PM when no party or coalition has a clear majority in the Lok Sabha, as in hung parliaments after 1989.

ex.q: Parliament sends the President a non-money bill. Trace what she can do and what follows.
st: She may sign it — it becomes law.
She may return it once for reconsideration.
If Parliament passes it again (with or without changes), she must give assent.
She may also simply not act on it for a long time — a pocket veto, since no time limit is fixed.
ex.a: Sign, return once (then must sign), or delay indefinitely (pocket veto). For a money bill she cannot return it.

topics.rl: After an election with no clear winner, all eyes turn to Rashtrapati Bhavan: the President's choice of whom to invite first can shape the next government.

topics.h: A government with 300 ministers? Not allowed. Since 2003 the Constitution caps the size of the ministry, after years of jumbo cabinets formed to keep allies happy.
p: The Vice-President is elected by members of both Houses of Parliament (STV), holds office for five years, is the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, and acts as President when the office falls vacant until a new President is elected.
The Prime Minister must have the support of a majority in the Lok Sabha. The President appoints as PM the person who commands this majority.
A person who is not a member of Parliament can become PM or a minister, but must become a member of either House within six months.
The PM chooses ministers and allocates portfolios. The 91st Amendment (2003) limits the Council of Ministers to 15% of the total membership of the Lok Sabha (or of the Assembly, in States).
Collective responsibility: the Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha. If the Lok Sabha passes a no-confidence motion, the entire ministry must resign.

ex.q: The Lok Sabha has 543 members. What is the maximum size of the Union Council of Ministers, including the PM?
st: The 91st Amendment caps it at 15% of the total Lok Sabha membership.
Ministers must be whole persons and cannot exceed 15%, so the maximum is 81.
ex.a: 81 ministers, including the Prime Minister.

topics.rl: Whenever a new ministry is sworn in at Rashtrapati Bhavan, analysts count heads to check it stays within the 15% cap of the 91st Amendment.

topics.t: Ministers, coalitions and the State executive
topics.h: Between 1989 and 2014, no single party won a Lok Sabha majority on its own. Prime Ministers had to run governments like captains of a team of many clubs.
p: The Council of Ministers has three ranks: Cabinet Ministers (senior leaders in charge of major ministries who form the Cabinet), Ministers of State (in charge of smaller ministries or assisting Cabinet ministers; some hold independent charge) and Deputy Ministers (assist ministers).
The Cabinet, the inner circle led by the PM, takes the main decisions; collective responsibility binds all ministers to support Cabinet decisions in public.
In coalition governments, the PM's power to choose ministers and set policy is limited by allies' demands; decisions need consultation and compromise.
With a single-party majority, the PM's dominance over the Cabinet and party tends to increase.
State executive: the Governor is appointed by the President and is the nominal head; the Chief Minister, who leads the majority in the Assembly, heads the Council of Ministers, the real executive.

ex.q: Compare the PM's power in a single-party majority government and in a coalition government.
st: Single-party majority: the PM chooses ministers freely and leads a disciplined party.
Coalition: allies demand ministries and influence policy; the PM must negotiate.
So coalition politics generally reduces the PM's freedom of action.
ex.a: The PM is more dominant with a single-party majority; coalition politics limits the PM's power.

topics.rl: When a state's Chief Minister presents the budget in the Vidhan Sabha while the Governor's address opens the session, you see real and nominal executive side by side.

topics.h: Ministers come and go, but the officers who run the railways, collect taxes and manage floods stay on. India's bureaucracy is one of the largest permanent workforces in the world.
p: The bureaucracy (civil service) is the permanent executive: trained and skilled officers who help ministers frame policy and implement it.
Civil servants are expected to be politically neutral: they serve whichever government is elected, without taking sides.

All India Services (e.g. IAS, IPS) are recruited by the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) and serve in States; there are also central services and State services (recruited by State Public Service Commissions).
Reservations in recruitment for SC, ST and OBC make the bureaucracy more representative of society.
Criticisms: red tape, insensitivity to ordinary citizens, and political interference (transfers, pressure). The Right to Information Act (2005) helps citizens hold officials accountable.

ex.q: Raju applies for a ration card and hears nothing for months. What can he do under the Right to Information Act?
st: File an RTI application asking the status of his application and the reasons for delay.
The office must reply within the time limit set by the Act.
This puts pressure on officials and exposes red tape.
ex.a: He can use RTI to seek information, making officials accountable.

topics.rl: Every year lakhs of aspirants sit for the UPSC Civil Services Examination; those selected for the IAS or IPS may later serve as District Collectors or Superintendents of Police in any State.

topics.h: Every rupee the government spends, from building AIIMS hospitals to buying fighter jets, must first be approved by Parliament. No vote, no money.
p: The legislature is the central forum of representative democracy: it makes laws, debates public issues, and holds the executive accountable.

Functions of Parliament: legislative (law-making), control of the executive, financial (approving taxes and spending), representative, debating, constituent (amending the Constitution), electoral (electing the President and Vice-President) and judicial (impeachment and removal of judges).
Parliament represents the divergent views of members from different regions, social groups and parties, making it the most representative organ.
Many observers note a decline of legislatures relative to the executive: strong cabinets, party discipline and less time for debate shift power towards the government.
Even so, the legislature remains the only place where every law and every rupee must be openly justified to the people's representatives.

ex.q: Classify each act of Parliament: (a) passing the Budget; (b) impeaching the President; (c) amending the Constitution; (d) electing the Vice-President.
st: (a) Approving taxes and spending → financial function.
(b) Removing the head of state for violation of the Constitution → judicial function.
(c) Changing the Constitution → constituent function.
(d) Choosing the Vice-President → electoral function.
ex.a: (a) Financial, (b) judicial, (c) constituent, (d) electoral.

topics.rl: When MPs from Ladakh, Kerala and Nagaland raise questions on the same day, Parliament acts as the meeting place of India's diversity.

topics.t: Two Houses: Rajya Sabha and Lok Sabha
topics.h: Uttar Pradesh sends 31 members to the Rajya Sabha, Sikkim sends 1. In the US Senate, California and Wyoming send 2 each. Which is fairer?
p: Bicameral legislature: two Houses. India's Parliament has the Rajya Sabha (Council of States) and the Lok Sabha (House of the People). Most States have a unicameral legislature; a few (e.g. Bihar, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh) also have a Legislative Council.

Rajya Sabha represents the States. Its members are elected indirectly by the elected members of State Legislative Assemblies (STV). It is a permanent House: never dissolved; members have six-year terms and one-third retire every two years.
Representation in the Rajya Sabha is based on population, so larger States get more seats (unequal representation), unlike the USA where every state has two Senators (equal representation).
The President nominates 12 members to the Rajya Sabha from among persons with special knowledge or experience in literature, science, art and social service.

Lok Sabha: directly elected by the people from territorial constituencies (543 seats), using FPTP; normal term five years, but it can be dissolved earlier if no government can be formed or on the PM's advice.

ex.q: A Rajya Sabha member's term began in April 2020. When will it end, and why are RS elections held every two years?
st: Each member's term is six years: April 2020 + 6 = April 2026.
One-third of members retire every two years, so elections are staggered.
Thus the House as a whole is never dissolved.
ex.a: April 2026; staggered retirement keeps the Rajya Sabha permanent.

topics.rl: Eminent people such as singer Lata Mangeshkar and cricketer Sachin Tendulkar have been nominated to the Rajya Sabha — the 12-nominee provision brings experience from outside politics into Parliament.

topics.h: The Rajya Sabha can debate the Budget for days — but it can't stop it. After 14 days, a money bill goes through anyway.
p: Exclusive powers of the Lok Sabha: money bills can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha; it approves the Budget; it alone can pass a no-confidence motion and remove the Council of Ministers.

Money bills: the Rajya Sabha can only discuss a money bill and suggest changes within 14 days; the Lok Sabha may accept or reject these suggestions. The Speaker decides whether a bill is a money bill.
On ordinary (non-money) bills, both Houses have equal powers; if they disagree, a joint sitting can be called.

Special powers of the Rajya Sabha: under Article 249 it can authorise Parliament, by a two-thirds resolution, to make laws on a State List subject in the national interest; it can also authorise the creation of new All India Services.
Overall, the Lok Sabha is more powerful because it represents the people directly and controls money and the ministry.

ex.q: The Lok Sabha passes a money bill on 1 March and sends it to the Rajya Sabha. The Rajya Sabha does nothing. What happens?
st: The Rajya Sabha must return a money bill with recommendations within 14 days.
If it does not return it within 14 days, the bill is deemed passed by both Houses.
So after 15 March the bill is deemed passed in the form passed by the Lok Sabha.
ex.a: The bill is deemed passed by both Houses after 14 days.

topics.rl: When the Finance Minister presents the Union Budget on 1 February, it is in the Lok Sabha that the Budget is presented and voted.

topics.h: A bill is like a train leaving a station: it must stop at several junctions — readings, committees, the other House, and Rashtrapati Bhavan — before it reaches its destination as an Act.
p: A bill is a draft of a proposed law. Government bills are introduced by ministers; private members' bills are introduced by MPs who are not ministers.
Money bills deal with taxes, borrowing and spending; they can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha. Non-money (ordinary) bills can be introduced in either House.

Stages: drafting by the ministry → introduction (first reading) → referral to a committee for detailed study → second reading (detailed, clause-by-clause consideration) → third reading (vote on the bill as a whole).
The bill then goes to the other House, which follows a similar process. If the Houses disagree on an ordinary bill, the President can summon a joint sitting, presided over by the Speaker.
Finally, the bill goes to the President for assent; once assent is given, the bill becomes an Act (law).

ex.q: Arrange the life of a government bill on road safety from idea to law.
st: The ministry drafts the bill after consultations.
A minister introduces it in a House (first reading).
It is referred to a committee, then debated clause by clause (second reading).
It is voted on (third reading), then passed by the other House.
The President gives assent and it becomes an Act.
ex.a: Draft → introduce → committee → clause-by-clause → vote → other House → assent → Act.

topics.rl: Every new traffic fine, tax change or consumer protection rule you read about began as a bill that crossed each of these junctions before the President signed it.

topics.h: The first hour of a Lok Sabha sitting belongs to MPs' questions. Ministers must answer — on rail accidents, prices, exam leaks, anything. It's called Question Hour.
p: Deliberation and discussion: Question Hour (MPs ask ministers questions), Zero Hour (members raise urgent matters, an Indian innovation), adjournment motions (to discuss a definite matter of urgent public importance), half-hour discussions and calling attention motions.
Approval and ratification: a government needs Parliament to pass its laws and policies, giving Parliament leverage over the executive.
Financial control: Parliament approves the Budget and demands for grants; the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) audits government accounts, and the Public Accounts Committee examines CAG reports.
No-confidence motion: the ultimate weapon; if passed by the Lok Sabha, the government must resign.
Limits: a government with a strong majority and strict party discipline may face weaker parliamentary control; frequent disruptions also reduce debate time.

ex.q: Match each situation to a tool: (a) MP wants the Railway Minister's answer on delays; (b) MPs want to set aside normal business to discuss a sudden flood; (c) the Opposition wants the government removed.
st: (a) Asking a minister a question → Question Hour.
(b) Urgent matter needing discussion → adjournment motion.
(c) Removing the government → no-confidence motion.
ex.a: (a) Question Hour, (b) adjournment motion, (c) no-confidence motion.

topics.rl: CAG audit reports on how public money was spent on projects and schemes are tabled in Parliament and examined by the Public Accounts Committee — that's financial control in action.

topics.t: Committees and how Parliament regulates itself
topics.h: A 300-page bill on data protection cannot be studied properly in a noisy House of 543. So Parliament sends it to a small committee of MPs from many parties who meet quietly, call experts and go clause by clause.
p: Standing committees are permanent; department-related standing committees scrutinise bills, demands for grants and the working of ministries. Ad hoc committees are set up for a specific purpose and end when their task is over.
Joint Parliamentary Committees (JPC) have members from both Houses and may be set up to examine a bill or investigate financial irregularities.
Committees allow detailed, less partisan study, and their reports guide the House.

The presiding officer (Speaker in the Lok Sabha, Chairman in the Rajya Sabha) is the final authority on conduct of business in the House. Members enjoy parliamentary privileges, e.g. no court action for anything said in the House.

Anti-defection law (52nd Amendment, 1985; Tenth Schedule): a member elected on a party ticket who leaves the party or defies the party whip can be disqualified; the presiding officer decides. The 91st Amendment (2003) tightened it by removing the 'split' exception.

ex.q: An MP elected on Party X's ticket votes against the party's whip in a crucial vote without permission. What can follow?
st: Defying the party whip without permission is ground for disqualification under the Tenth Schedule.
The party can petition the presiding officer.
The Speaker or Chairman decides whether the member is disqualified.
ex.a: He can be disqualified under the anti-defection law, as decided by the presiding officer.

topics.rl: Bills on data protection, forests and criminal law have been sent to Joint or Standing Committees, where MPs from rival parties sit around one table and invite experts and citizens' groups.

topics.t: Why the judiciary must be independent
topics.h: A cricket umpire who could be sacked by the batting side would never give anyone out. Judges deciding cases against the government face the same problem — unless they are independent.
p: The judiciary settles disputes between citizens, between citizens and government, and between governments; it protects rights and upholds the rule of law.
Independence means the other organs (legislature and executive) must not interfere with the judiciary's work, so judges can decide without fear or favour.
Independence does not mean arbitrariness or absence of accountability: the judiciary is accountable to the Constitution, democratic traditions and the people.

Safeguards: the legislature is not involved in appointing judges; judges have a fixed tenure and retirement age (65 for Supreme Court, 62 for High Court judges) and can be removed only by a very difficult procedure.

Judges' salaries and allowances are charged on the Consolidated Fund and not voted on by the legislature; judges' decisions cannot be criticised on personal grounds, and courts can punish for contempt of court.

ex.q: A State government is unhappy with a High Court judgment. Ministers propose cutting the judges' salaries. Can they? Explain.
st: Judges' salaries are charged expenditure and are not subject to a vote of the legislature.
The Constitution forbids reducing judges' salaries to their disadvantage during their tenure (except in a financial emergency).
So the government cannot punish judges by cutting their pay — this protects independence.
ex.a: No; financial security of judges is a constitutional safeguard of independence.

topics.rl: When the Supreme Court strikes down a government decision, ministers must comply even if they dislike it — that is the rule of law, guarded by an independent judiciary.

topics.h: Only once has a motion to remove a Supreme Court judge been put to the vote in the Lok Sabha — and it failed. Removing a judge is meant to be very hard.
p: The President appoints the Chief Justice of India and other judges. By convention, the senior-most judge of the Supreme Court is appointed CJI; this convention was broken in 1973 when Justice A.N. Ray was appointed over three senior judges, and again later in the 1970s.

Collegium system: following Supreme Court judgments, appointments are recommended by the CJI along with the four senior-most judges of the Supreme Court, and the executive formally makes the appointment.

Debate: some argue the executive should have a bigger say (accountability); others say judicial primacy protects independence. The judiciary has the main say in recommending names, while the Council of Ministers has a role in the formal appointment.

Removal: a judge can be removed only on the ground of proven misbehaviour or incapacity, by a motion passed by a special majority (majority of total membership and two-thirds of members present and voting) in both Houses.
This procedure is rarely used; the motion against Justice V. Ramaswami (early 1990s) failed in Parliament.

ex.q: A removal motion is moved in the Lok Sabha (543 members). On the day of voting, 450 members are present and voting. What is needed to pass it?
st: Condition 1: majority of total membership → more than 543 ÷ 2, i.e. at least 272.
Condition 2: two-thirds of those present and voting → 2/3 × 450 = 300.
Both must be met, so at least 300 votes are needed (300 is also more than 272).
Then the Rajya Sabha must pass it by the same kind of special majority.
ex.a: At least 300 votes in the Lok Sabha, and a similar special majority in the Rajya Sabha.

topics.rl: When the Supreme Court collegium publishes its recommendations online, newspapers track whether the government notifies the appointments — the appointment debate plays out in real time.

topics.h: A land dispute in a village in Odisha can travel from a District Court to the Orissa High Court and finally to the Supreme Court in New Delhi — one single ladder of courts for the whole country.
p: India has a single integrated judicial system: unlike some federations, there are no separate State and federal court systems.
Supreme Court: the highest court; its decisions are binding on all courts in India; it can transfer cases and hear appeals from High Courts.
High Courts: hear appeals from lower courts; issue writs for Fundamental Rights and other purposes; supervise and control subordinate courts in the State.
District Courts: deal with civil and criminal cases arising in the district and hear appeals from lower courts; subordinate courts handle cases at the lowest level.
Because the Supreme Court sits at the top, its interpretation of the law creates uniformity across the country.

ex.q: Trace the appeal route of a criminal case decided by a Sessions Court in Nagpur.
st: The Sessions Court is a district-level court.
Appeal lies to the High Court of the State (Bombay High Court, Nagpur Bench).
Further appeal can lie to the Supreme Court.
ex.a: District/Sessions Court → High Court → Supreme Court.

topics.rl: When the Supreme Court decides how a law should be read, every judge from Leh to Kanyakumari must follow it — that's the power of an integrated judiciary.

topics.h: A boundary dispute between two States, a citizen's plea against illegal detention, an appeal in a murder case, and the President asking for legal advice — all can land at the same building on Tilak Marg, New Delhi.
p: Original jurisdiction: cases that go directly to the Supreme Court, without passing through lower courts — disputes between the Union and States, or between States. (Inter-State river water disputes are an exception: Parliament has provided for tribunals to settle them.)
Writ jurisdiction: any person whose Fundamental Right is violated can move the Supreme Court directly (Article 32). High Courts can also issue writs (Article 226), and for wider purposes.
Appellate jurisdiction: the Supreme Court is the highest court of appeal in civil, criminal and constitutional cases.
Advisory jurisdiction (Article 143): the President can refer a question of law or public importance for the Court's opinion; the Court may decline, and its advice is not binding on the President.
Special powers: special leave to appeal against any judgment of any court (Article 136), and the power to pass any order to do 'complete justice' (Article 142).

ex.q: Identify the jurisdiction: (a) two neighbouring States dispute the boundary between them; (b) a person detained illegally files a petition; (c) the President asks for the Court's view on a legal question.
st: (a) A dispute between States goes directly to the Supreme Court → original jurisdiction.
(b) Violation of a Fundamental Right → writ jurisdiction (Article 32).
(c) Opinion sought by the President → advisory jurisdiction (Article 143).
ex.a: (a) Original, (b) writ, (c) advisory.

topics.rl: Article 142 has been used by the Supreme Court to give directions in matters as varied as environmental protection and settling long-pending disputes — a power to do 'complete justice'.

topics.h: In 1979, newspaper reports revealed that thousands of undertrial prisoners in Bihar had spent longer in jail than the maximum sentence for their alleged crimes. A petition on their behalf changed Indian law forever.
p: Public Interest Litigation (PIL): the courts relaxed the rule of locus standi, so a person or group can approach the court on behalf of those whose rights are violated, even if they are not personally affected.

Origins: late 1970s and early 1980s. Hussainara Khatoon (1979) concerned undertrial prisoners in Bihar; the Court later also accepted letters and newspaper reports as petitions, e.g. on prisoners' rights and bonded labour.
Positive effects: access to justice for the poor and voiceless; greater accountability of the executive; courts gave directions on issues like environment, bonded labour, and prison conditions.
Criticism: courts become overburdened; the line between judiciary, executive and legislature blurs (separation of powers), as courts take up executive tasks; some decisions are hard to implement.
Judicial activism is the broad term for this active role of courts in protecting rights and public interest.

ex.q: Five bonded labourers in a stone quarry cannot afford a lawyer. An NGO hears of them. How can the court help?
st: Under traditional rules, only an affected person could go to court (locus standi).
Through PIL, the NGO can file a petition on behalf of the labourers.
The court can examine the case and order their release and rehabilitation.
ex.a: The NGO files a PIL; the court, using relaxed locus standi, protects the labourers' rights.

topics.rl: PILs have led courts to issue orders on Delhi's air pollution, cleaning the Ganga and the rights of street vendors — showing both the reach and the debate around judicial activism.

topics.h: Can Parliament, elected by crores, pass any law it likes? In 1973, thirteen judges of the Supreme Court gave an answer that still shapes Indian democracy.
p: Judicial review: the power of courts to examine whether a law (or executive action) is consistent with the Constitution, and to declare it invalid if it is not.
The judiciary protects rights through writs (habeas corpus, mandamus, etc.) and by striking down laws that violate Fundamental Rights.
Conflict with Parliament: over the right to property and Parliament's power to amend Fundamental Rights. In Golaknath (1967), the Court said Parliament could not amend Fundamental Rights.

In Kesavananda Bharati (1973), the Court held that Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights, but cannot alter its 'basic structure'. This doctrine limits Parliament's amending power.
Other tensions: privileges of the legislature versus judicial review; Parliament cannot discuss judges' conduct except in removal proceedings, and courts can punish contempt.

ex.q: Parliament passes an amendment saying that courts cannot examine any future law at all. How would the courts view this?
st: Judicial review is considered part of the basic structure of the Constitution.
Under Kesavananda Bharati, Parliament cannot amend the basic structure.
So the courts would likely strike down such an amendment.
ex.a: It would be struck down as violating the basic structure (judicial review).

topics.rl: When the Supreme Court tests a new law against the Constitution, it is using judicial review — the same power that let it uphold or strike down laws on issues from privacy to elections.

topics.h: In 1991 the Soviet Union, a giant federation, broke into 15 independent countries. India, even more diverse, has held together. Structure alone can't explain the difference — spirit matters.
p: Federalism is an institutional arrangement with two (or more) levels of government: one for the whole country and others for regions (States, provinces), with powers divided between them by the constitution.

Key features: two sets of government with their own powers; a written constitution that divides powers and cannot be changed by one level alone; an independent judiciary to settle disputes between levels.

Federations can fail when diversity is not respected or power is too concentrated: the Soviet Union broke up in 1991; the West Indies Federation (1958) dissolved within a few years; Nigeria faced civil war and military rule.
Federalism suits large, diverse societies because it allows unity with diversity, but it works only if there is a federal spirit: mutual trust, respect and willingness to share power.
Each federation is shaped by its history: some formed when independent units came together, others when a large country divided powers among regions.

ex.q: A country has a central government and State governments, but the central government can abolish any State government by an ordinary order. Is it federal?
st: In a federation, each level has constitutionally guaranteed powers.
If one level can abolish the other at will, the powers are not guaranteed.
So the arrangement is not truly federal; it is closer to a unitary system.
ex.a: No — without constitutional guarantee of each level's powers, it is not a true federation.

topics.rl: When your State government runs the police and the Union government runs the railways, you're seeing federalism's division of powers every day.

topics.t: The Union of States and the three lists
topics.h: Who decides on your school syllabus, the police in your city, and the trains you ride? The answer is written in three lists in the Seventh Schedule.
p: Article 1 says 'India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States'. The word 'federation' is not used.

The Seventh Schedule divides legislative powers into three lists: Union List (subjects of national importance), State List (subjects of local and regional importance) and Concurrent List (subjects on which both can make laws).

Union List examples: defence, foreign affairs, banking, atomic energy, currency, railways, posts and telegraphs. State List examples: police, public order, agriculture, public health, local government, trade within the State.
Concurrent List examples: education, forests, marriage, adoption, succession, trade unions, criminal law. If a Union law and a State law on a concurrent subject conflict, the Union law prevails.
Residuary powers (subjects not in any list) belong to the Union, e.g. new areas like cyber laws.

ex.q: Classify: (a) defence; (b) police; (c) education; (d) a brand-new subject not in any list.
st: (a) National security → Union List.
(b) Law and order is regional → State List.
(c) Both make laws → Concurrent List.
(d) Not in any list → residuary, with the Union.
ex.a: (a) Union, (b) State, (c) Concurrent, (d) Union (residuary).

topics.rl: The National Education Policy is framed by the Centre, while State boards set many syllabi — education being on the Concurrent List lets both act.

topics.t: A federation with a strong Centre
topics.h: Parliament can create a new State, rename an old one or redraw its borders — and the State's own legislature cannot veto it. Few federations give their centre such power.
p: Reasons for a strong Centre: the trauma of Partition, the need to integrate over 500 princely states, and the need for the Centre to lead economic development and social change.
Article 3: Parliament can form new States, alter boundaries or change names by law; the President must seek the views of the State legislature, but those views are not binding.
Emergency provisions turn the system almost unitary: during a national emergency, Parliament can make laws on State subjects and the Centre can give directions to States.

Financial dependence: the Centre controls major sources of revenue; States depend on grants and tax shares. The Finance Commission (Article 280), appointed every five years, recommends distribution of taxes between Centre and States.
Other powers: Governors (appointed by the President) can reserve State bills for the President's consideration; All India Services officers serve in States but are controlled by the Centre.

ex.q: Parliament passes a law changing the boundary of State X. The State legislature opposes it. Is the law valid?
st: Article 3 lets Parliament alter boundaries by law.
The President must refer the bill to the State legislature for its views.
The State's views are not binding, so the law is valid even if the State opposes it.
ex.a: Yes, it is valid — the State's opposition does not bind Parliament.

topics.rl: When a State asks the Finance Commission for a bigger share of central taxes after a cyclone or drought, you see the financial dependence of States on the Centre.

topics.h: Between the 1950s and the 1990s, State governments were dismissed and President's Rule imposed many times — sometimes for reasons the Supreme Court later called improper.
p: Centre–State relations changed over time: in the early decades one party ruled at the Centre and in most States; from the late 1960s and especially after 1989, different parties and coalitions led States and the Centre, and regional parties became more assertive.

Demands for autonomy: more powers to States (political), more financial resources (financial), control over administrative services (administrative), and protection of language and culture (cultural/linguistic).
Governor's role: appointed by the Centre, the Governor is often seen as acting for the ruling party at the Centre, especially in recommending President's Rule.

Article 356 (President's Rule): if the constitutional machinery in a State fails, the Centre can take over the State's government; it has been misused at times. In S.R. Bommai (1994) the Supreme Court ruled that such dismissal is subject to judicial review and majority must be tested on the floor of the House.
The Sarkaria Commission (set up in 1983) examined Centre–State relations and recommended that Governors be appointed in a non-partisan way.

ex.q: A Governor recommends dismissing a State government, saying it has lost majority, without allowing a floor test. What does the S.R. Bommai judgment say?
st: Bommai held that the majority of a government must be tested on the floor of the Assembly.
It also held that a proclamation under Article 356 is subject to judicial review.
So dismissing the government without a floor test can be challenged in court.
ex.a: The government's majority must be tested on the floor; the dismissal can be reviewed by courts.

topics.rl: When a State asks for its fair share of GST compensation or tax devolution, it is making a financial autonomy demand — a recurring theme in Centre–State relations.

topics.h: In November 2000, three new States were born in just two weeks: Chhattisgarh, Uttarakhand and Jharkhand. Fourteen years later, Telangana became the 29th State.
p: Linguistic reorganisation: after demands and movements, many States were reorganised on the basis of language, especially through the States Reorganisation Act of 1956.

Demands for new States continued for reasons of identity, development and better administration. In 2000, Chhattisgarh (from Madhya Pradesh), Uttarakhand (from Uttar Pradesh) and Jharkhand (from Bihar) were created; Telangana was carved out of Andhra Pradesh in 2014.
Border disputes between States: e.g. Belgaum (Belagavi), claimed by Maharashtra and Karnataka; Chandigarh, claimed by both Punjab and Haryana and serving as the capital of both.
River water disputes: e.g. the Cauvery dispute between Karnataka and Tamil Nadu (with Kerala and Puducherry also involved), and the Narmada dispute involving Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh and Maharashtra.
Such disputes are settled through negotiation, tribunals and the courts, showing how federalism manages conflict peacefully.

ex.q: Match the new State to its parent State: Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Uttarakhand, Telangana.
st: Jharkhand ← Bihar (2000).
Chhattisgarh ← Madhya Pradesh (2000).
Uttarakhand ← Uttar Pradesh (2000).
Telangana ← Andhra Pradesh (2014).
ex.a: Jharkhand–Bihar, Chhattisgarh–MP, Uttarakhand–UP, Telangana–AP.

topics.rl: Farmers in Karnataka and Tamil Nadu both watch Cauvery water releases closely during the monsoon — a dispute managed through tribunals and courts.

topics.h: In Nagaland, certain Acts of Parliament on Naga customary law and land ownership don't apply unless the State Assembly agrees. Not all States are treated exactly alike — by design.
p: Asymmetric federalism: the Constitution makes special provisions for some States because of their history, culture or special circumstances.

Article 371 and related Articles (371A–371J) give special provisions for many States, including North-Eastern States (e.g. Nagaland, Mizoram, Assam, Manipur, Arunachal Pradesh, Sikkim) and others such as Maharashtra, Gujarat, Andhra Pradesh, Goa and Karnataka.
For Nagaland and Mizoram, Acts of Parliament on religious and social practices, customary law and ownership of land do not apply unless the State Assembly decides so.

Jammu and Kashmir had special status under Article 370. In August 2019 this special status was ended, and through the Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019, the State was reorganised into two Union Territories: Jammu and Kashmir, and Ladakh.
Special provisions show that Indian federalism accommodates diversity rather than forcing uniformity.

ex.q: Classify these as features of 'symmetric' or 'asymmetric' federalism: (a) all States share the same three lists; (b) special protection of customary law in Nagaland.
st: (a) Applies equally to all States → symmetric feature.
(b) Applies only to certain States due to their special circumstances → asymmetric feature.
ex.a: (a) Symmetric; (b) asymmetric.

topics.rl: Autonomous District Councils in tribal areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram (under the Sixth Schedule) and protections for tribal land are reminders that Indian federalism adapts to regional needs.

topics.h: Your street light is broken, the village pond is silting up, and the primary school needs a new toilet. Would you rather wait for Delhi, or walk to your panchayat office?
p: Local government is government at the village and district level (panchayats) and the town and city level (municipalities). It is the level of government closest to ordinary people.
It deals with everyday matters: drinking water, sanitation, local roads, primary schools, street lights, markets.
Benefits: people can participate directly; local knowledge leads to better decisions; problems are solved faster and more cheaply; it deepens democracy through democratic decentralisation.
Decentralisation means transferring powers and resources from higher levels of government to local bodies.
