ex.q: A critic says: 'Secularism is anti-religious.' Give the reply.
st: Secularism opposes domination by or within religions.
It protects every person's freedom to practise religion.
So it is not against religion, only against religious domination.
ex.a: Secularism opposes religious domination, not religion; it protects religious freedom.

topics.rl: Public debates on whether a government policy is 'appeasement' or 'protection of minorities' are versions of the minoritism criticism and its reply.

qa.q: What is the most basic reason a society needs a constitution?
qa.a: To provide a set of basic rules that allow minimal coordination and trust among its members
qa.e: A constitution lays down basic rules so members of a diverse society can coordinate and trust each other.

qa.q: A constitution provides 'assurance' to the members of a society. What does this mean?
qa.a: Each member knows the minimum rules that every other member must also follow
qa.e: Assurance means you can trust that others are bound by the same basic rules.

qa.q: Which of the following is the FIRST function of a constitution as described in your book?
qa.a: Specifying the basic allocation of power: who gets to make decisions
qa.e: The first function is to specify who has the power to make decisions in a society. Limits and identity are other functions.

qa.q: The Indian Constitution says that, in most matters, Parliament gets to decide laws and policies. This is an example of a constitution
qa.a: deciding who has the authority to make decisions
qa.e: Giving law-making power to Parliament is the allocation of decision-making authority.

qa.q: In a thought experiment, a new island society has no agreed basic rules. What is the most likely result?
qa.a: Constant disputes, because nobody can trust how others will behave or who decides
qa.e: Without basic rules there is no coordination or assurance, so disagreements cannot be settled peacefully.

qa.q: Why must the constitution also say how the decision-making body itself is constituted (for example, how Parliament is organised)?
qa.a: Because people need to know not just who decides but how that body is formed, so its decisions are accepted
qa.e: Specifying how the authority is constituted gives it legitimacy and makes its decisions acceptable.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A constitution creates trust among the members of a society. Reason (R): It lays down basic rules that every member knows others must also follow.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Trust comes precisely from the shared, known minimum rules, so R explains A.

qa.q: Which of these is NOT a reason why a large, diverse society needs a constitution?
qa.a: To ensure that all members hold the same religious beliefs
qa.e: A constitution allows people with different beliefs to live together; it does not require everyone to share one belief.

qa.q: A government passes a law forbidding citizens from forming any associations. Which function of a constitution would be most clearly violated?
qa.a: Setting limits on what the government can impose on citizens
qa.e: Freedom of association is a fundamental limit on government; a law ignoring it crosses that limit.

qa.q: Which of the following is the most common way in which constitutions limit government power?
qa.a: By specifying fundamental rights that the government may not violate
qa.e: Rights are the standard way of drawing lines government cannot cross.

qa.q: The Indian Constitution empowers the government to take positive measures to overcome long-standing caste discrimination. This reflects which function?
qa.a: Enabling the government to fulfil the aspirations of society and create a just society
qa.e: Here the constitution does not restrain the state; it directs and enables it to bring about justice.

qa.q: 'Through a constitution, a people express their fundamental identity.' This means that
qa.a: agreeing on basic norms makes people a single political community with a shared collective identity
qa.e: A political community is formed when people accept shared basic rules and principles, not by uniformity of language or faith.

qa.q: How does the Indian Constitution treat the relationship between national identity and other identities such as religion or language?
qa.a: National identity does not depend on any one religion or language; it accommodates many identities
qa.e: India's constitutional identity is civic and plural; it accommodates diverse identities.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Fundamental rights are a means by which a constitution limits government. Reason (R): Even an elected government can never violate fundamental rights without facing constitutional checks.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true, and the fact that elected governments too are bound is exactly why rights act as limits.

qa.q: Which pair correctly matches a provision with its function?
qa.a: Protection against arbitrary arrest — limits government power
qa.e: Protection against arbitrary arrest restrains the state, so it is a limit.

qa.q: A constitution that only allocated power and set limits, but gave the state no role in reducing deep social inequalities, would be missing which function?
qa.a: Enabling the government to fulfil society's aspirations for justice
qa.e: The third function is the enabling, transformative role of a constitution.

qa.q: Which of these is NOT a factor that gives a constitution effective authority, as discussed in your book?
qa.a: The number of pages it has
qa.e: Length has nothing to do with authority; how it was made, what it says and how it is designed matter.

qa.q: 'Mode of promulgation' refers to
qa.a: how a constitution came into being and who drafted it
qa.e: Promulgation concerns who wrote the constitution and with how much popular credibility.

qa.q: Why does a constitution drafted by a popularly backed assembly carry more authority than one imposed by an unpopular ruler?
qa.a: People accept it as legitimate because it was made by those they trust and who represent them
qa.e: Legitimacy flows from the credibility of those who made it.

qa.q: A constitution protects the rights of only one community and denies them to others. Which source of authority is weakest in this case?
qa.a: Substantive provisions
qa.e: If the content is unfair to many groups, they have no reason to accept it.

qa.q: What does 'balanced institutional design' require?
qa.a: Power is distributed among institutions that check one another, so no single group can subvert the constitution
qa.e: Balance means separation and checks, plus the right mix of rigidity and flexibility.

qa.q: Which statement about rigidity and flexibility is most accurate?
qa.a: A good constitution protects core values from easy change but allows amendment to adapt to new circumstances
qa.e: Too rigid and it breaks under new needs; too flexible and core values are lost.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Many constitutions in the world have been suspended or set aside within a few years of being made. Reason (R): They often lacked popular credibility, fair provisions or balanced institutions.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true, and these weaknesses are exactly why such constitutions lost authority.

qa.q: The word 'constitution' can refer to the written document. What else can it mean?
qa.a: The working body of rules and practices by which a country is actually governed
qa.e: Some countries, like the UK, have no single document but still have a constitution in the sense of a working body of rules.

qa.q: On which date did the Constituent Assembly hold its first meeting?
qa.a: 9 December 1946
qa.e: The first sitting was on 9 December 1946.

qa.q: How were the members of the Constituent Assembly chosen?
qa.a: Indirectly, by members of the provincial legislative assemblies
qa.e: Under the Cabinet Mission scheme, provincial legislators elected the members.

qa.q: Under whose scheme was the Constituent Assembly composed?
qa.a: The Cabinet Mission (1946)
qa.e: The Cabinet Mission plan of 1946 set out how the Assembly would be formed.

qa.q: Roughly how many people did each seat in the Constituent Assembly represent?
qa.a: About 10 lakh (one million)
qa.e: Seats were allotted roughly in proportion to population, one seat per million.

qa.q: Which three communities were recognised for dividing a province's seats in the Assembly?
qa.a: Muslims, Sikhs and General
qa.e: The Cabinet Mission recognised only these three categories; 'General' included all others.

qa.q: The Constitution of India was adopted on ___ and came into force on ___.
qa.a: 26 November 1949; 26 January 1950
qa.e: Adoption (26 Nov 1949) came first; commencement (26 Jan 1950) came two months later.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The Constituent Assembly represented a wide range of opinions even though the Congress dominated it. Reason (R): The Congress itself was a broad platform that included people of many ideological views, and members from other groups were also included.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the Congress's own diversity plus other members explains the variety of views.

qa.q: Critics say the Assembly was 'not representative'. Which fact is the basis of this criticism?
qa.a: Its members were not elected by universal adult franchise
qa.e: The criticism rests on indirect election, since universal franchise did not exist in 1946.

qa.q: Who chaired the Drafting Committee of the Constituent Assembly?
qa.a: Dr B.R. Ambedkar
qa.e: Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee; Rajendra Prasad was President of the Assembly.

qa.q: Who moved the Objectives Resolution in the Constituent Assembly in 1946?
qa.a: Jawaharlal Nehru
qa.e: Nehru moved it in December 1946; it set out the Assembly's aims.

qa.q: Which of the following was a principle of the Objectives Resolution?
qa.a: All power and authority of independent India would be derived from the people
qa.e: Popular sovereignty was central to the Resolution, later reflected in 'We, the people'.

qa.q: Which document of 1928 demanded a bill of rights for Indians?
qa.a: The Motilal Nehru Report
qa.e: The Nehru Report (1928) is an early demand for rights; Karachi came in 1931.

qa.q: How did the Constituent Assembly generally take decisions?
qa.a: Through deliberation and an effort to build consensus
qa.e: The Assembly valued open public reasoning and broad agreement.

qa.q: Many administrative and institutional details of the Constitution were drawn from
qa.a: the Government of India Act 1935
qa.e: The 1935 Act provided much of the administrative structure.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The Indian Constitution drew strength from the national movement. Reason (R): Demands for rights and democracy had been made by nationalist leaders in documents like the Nehru Report (1928) and the Karachi Resolution (1931).
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; these earlier demands are why the Constitution is said to inherit the national movement's ideals.

qa.q: Which statement best describes how the Assembly approached institutional design?
qa.a: It balanced powers among legislature, executive, judiciary and between Centre and states
qa.e: Balancing institutions was a central concern so that no organ would dominate.

qa.q: Why is the Indian Constitution described as a living framework rather than a frozen rulebook?
qa.a: It embodies democratic values and can adapt through amendment and interpretation while keeping its core
qa.e: The Constitution carries the democratic values of the national movement and can be adapted to new needs, but its core principles stay protected.

qa.q: The Directive Principles of State Policy were adapted from the constitution of
qa.a: Ireland
qa.e: The Irish Constitution is the source of DPSP.

qa.q: Which feature was taken from the United States Constitution?
qa.a: Judicial review
qa.e: Judicial review, a charter of rights and an independent judiciary came from the USA.

qa.q: The principles of liberty, equality and fraternity were drawn from the
qa.a: French Constitution
qa.e: These are the ideals of the French Revolution.

qa.q: The idea of a quasi-federal government with a strong Centre and residual powers with the Centre was taken from
qa.a: Canada
qa.e: Canada's model combines federalism with a strong centre and residual powers at the Centre.

qa.q: Which set is entirely British in origin?
qa.a: FPTP, rule of law, the Speaker's institution, law-making procedure
qa.e: Judicial review and fundamental rights came from the USA; DPSP from Ireland.

qa.q: What is the best way to describe the use of foreign provisions by the Constitution makers?
qa.a: They adapted ideas to Indian needs and conditions instead of blindly copying them
qa.e: The makers studied many constitutions and reshaped ideas for India.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The makers of the Indian Constitution did not blindly copy foreign provisions. Reason (R): They examined borrowed ideas and adapted them to Indian conditions and to the ideals of the national movement.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true, and the process of adaptation is exactly why the borrowing was not blind copying.

qa.q: A student matches 'Independence of the judiciary — Ireland'. What is the correct source?
qa.a: United States
qa.e: Independence of the judiciary is listed with US-derived features; Ireland gave DPSP.

qa.q: What is a 'Bill of Rights'?
qa.a: A list of rights written into a constitution and protected from violation
qa.e: A Bill of Rights is a constitutional list of guaranteed rights.

qa.q: How are Fundamental Rights different from ordinary legal rights?
qa.a: Fundamental Rights can be changed only by amending the Constitution, while legal rights can be changed by ordinary law
qa.e: Fundamental Rights have higher protection; ordinary legislation cannot take them away.

qa.q: Which statement about Fundamental Rights is correct?
qa.a: They are not absolute; the state can impose reasonable restrictions
qa.e: Rights are balanced against public order, morality, security and others' rights.

qa.q: Why is the existence of remedies an essential part of a bill of rights?
qa.a: Without a way to enforce rights in court, rights would be only promises on paper
qa.e: Enforceability makes rights real; Article 32 provides it.

qa.q: Rights protect an individual against
qa.a: both the state and other individuals or groups
qa.e: Rights restrain government and also protect people from domination by others.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The Indian Constitution gives Fundamental Rights special protection. Reason (R): They can be changed only by a constitutional amendment, not by ordinary law.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true; the amendment requirement is what gives them special protection.

qa.q: In which Part of the Constitution are the Fundamental Rights listed?
qa.a: Part III
qa.e: Part III has Fundamental Rights; Part IV has DPSP; Part IVA has Fundamental Duties.

qa.q: Which demand of the freedom struggle is an early sign of the call for constitutional rights?
qa.a: The Motilal Nehru Report (1928) demanding a bill of rights
qa.e: The Nehru Report was an Indian demand for rights; the others were British measures.

qa.q: Which Article guarantees 'equality before the law' and 'equal protection of the laws'?
qa.a: Article 14
qa.e: Article 14 is the general equality clause.

qa.q: Article 17 of the Indian Constitution deals with
qa.a: abolition of untouchability
qa.e: Article 17 abolishes untouchability; Article 18 abolishes titles.

qa.q: A state government advertises posts saying that only men may apply, with no special reason. Which right is most directly violated?
qa.a: Equality of opportunity in public employment (Article 16)
qa.e: Article 16 forbids discrimination, including on grounds of sex, in public employment.

qa.q: Which of the following is permitted under the Right to Equality?
qa.a: Special provisions for socially and educationally backward classes
qa.e: Articles 15 and 16 allow special provisions for disadvantaged groups to achieve real equality.

qa.q: Under Article 18, which of the following can the state still confer?
qa.a: A military or academic distinction
qa.e: Article 18 abolishes titles except military and academic distinctions.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Reservation in government jobs for backward classes is consistent with the Right to Equality. Reason (R): Equality includes equal opportunity, and special measures for disadvantaged groups help achieve it.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the Constitution sees special measures as a way to achieve real equality of opportunity.

qa.q: The grounds on which Article 15 forbids the state to discriminate are
qa.a: religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth
qa.e: These five grounds are listed in Article 15.

qa.q: A district collector is accused of a crime. She claims she cannot be tried by an ordinary court because of her rank. Which principle rejects her claim?
qa.a: Equality before the law (Article 14)
qa.e: Article 14 means no person, however senior, is above the law.

qa.q: How many freedoms does Article 19 currently guarantee to citizens?
qa.e: Speech, assembly, association, movement, residence and profession: six freedoms.

qa.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the freedoms under Article 19?
qa.a: Freedom to assemble with arms
qa.e: Article 19 protects peaceful assembly without arms.

qa.q: Article 21 states that no person shall be deprived of life or personal liberty except
qa.a: according to procedure established by law
qa.e: Only a lawful procedure can deprive a person of life or liberty.

qa.q: Which of the following has the Supreme Court read into the right to life under Article 21?
qa.a: The right to livelihood and shelter
qa.e: Courts interpret life as a life with dignity, including shelter and livelihood.

qa.q: Which amendment made free and compulsory education for children aged 6–14 a Fundamental Right?
qa.a: 86th Amendment (2002)
qa.e: The 86th Amendment inserted Article 21A.

qa.q: A state bans a protest march because organisers plan to carry swords. Is this a valid restriction?
qa.a: Yes, because Article 19 protects only peaceful assembly without arms
qa.e: Assembly must be peaceful and unarmed; public order allows restriction.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The right to life and personal liberty under Article 21 is available to non-citizens in India too. Reason (R): Article 21 protects every 'person', while Article 19 freedoms are given only to citizens.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the word 'person' in Article 21 is exactly why foreigners in India are also protected.

qa.q: Which freedom was once in Article 19 but no longer is?
qa.a: Freedom to acquire, hold and dispose of property
qa.e: The property freedom was removed by the 44th Amendment.

qa.q: Within how many hours must an arrested person be produced before the nearest magistrate (excluding travel time)?
qa.e: Article 22 sets the 24-hour limit.

qa.q: The principle that no person can be prosecuted and punished more than once for the same offence is called
qa.a: protection against double jeopardy
qa.e: Article 20 forbids double punishment for the same offence.

qa.q: Police force an accused to sign a confession against himself. Which right is violated?
qa.a: Right against self-incrimination
qa.e: No person accused of an offence can be compelled to be a witness against himself.

qa.q: What is preventive detention?
qa.a: Detaining a person because the government fears he may commit an act harmful to law and order or national security
qa.e: It is preventive: it aims to stop a feared future act.

qa.q: A new law makes an act punishable that was legal when it was done last year. Can a person be punished for last year's act?
qa.a: No, because no one can be punished for an act that was not an offence when it was committed
qa.e: Article 20 bars retrospective criminal punishment.

qa.q: What is the main criticism of preventive detention laws?
qa.a: They can be misused by governments to curb dissent and detain opponents
qa.e: Possible misuse is the central concern.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Preventive detention laws have been widely criticised. Reason (R): They allow a person to be detained without having committed an offence, which can be misused against opponents.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the risk of detaining people without a proven offence is the reason for the criticism.

qa.q: Which safeguard applies to a person held under preventive detention?
qa.a: Detention beyond the initial period requires review by an advisory board
qa.e: The Constitution provides review by an advisory board and communication of grounds.

qa.q: What does 'begar' mean?
qa.a: Forced labour without payment
qa.e: Begar is compulsory unpaid labour, banned under Article 23.

qa.q: Article 24 prohibits employment of children below what age in factories, mines and hazardous work?
qa.a: 14 years
qa.e: The constitutional age limit is 14.

qa.q: Which of the following is part of the Right to Freedom of Religion?
qa.a: Freedom to profess, practise and propagate religion
qa.e: Article 25 guarantees freedom of conscience and the right to profess, practise and propagate religion.

qa.q: A school fully funded by the state starts compulsory religious lessons for all students. This violates
qa.a: the Right to Freedom of Religion
qa.e: Article 28 bars religious instruction in institutions wholly maintained by the state.

qa.q: Who can establish and administer educational institutions under Article 30?
qa.a: All minorities, whether based on religion or language
qa.e: Article 30 covers both religious and linguistic minorities.

qa.q: Can the state make laws to reform social practices associated with religion?
qa.a: Yes, it can regulate secular activities linked to religion and make social reforms
qa.e: Freedom of religion does not stop social reform laws or regulation of secular aspects.

qa.q: Assertion (A): India is described as a secular state. Reason (R): The Constitution does not establish any official religion and gives freedom to all religions.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the absence of a state religion plus freedom for all is what makes India secular.

qa.q: Trafficking of women and children for forced work violates which right?
qa.a: Right against Exploitation
qa.e: Article 23 bans traffic in human beings.

qa.q: Which right did Dr Ambedkar describe as the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution?
qa.a: Right to Constitutional Remedies
qa.e: Without remedies, other rights cannot be enforced, so Ambedkar gave Article 32 this place.

qa.q: A person is detained by the police without being produced before a magistrate. Which writ will help him most directly?
qa.a: Habeas corpus
qa.e: Habeas corpus orders the detained person to be produced before the court.

qa.q: The writ of mandamus is issued when
qa.a: a public official fails to perform a legal duty
qa.e: Mandamus means 'we command'; it orders performance of duty.

qa.q: Which writ asks 'by what authority' a person holds a public office?
qa.a: Quo warranto
qa.e: Quo warranto challenges an unlawful claim to office.

qa.q: A higher court orders a lower court to stop hearing a case that is outside its jurisdiction. This writ is
qa.a: prohibition
qa.e: Prohibition stops proceedings beyond jurisdiction; certiorari transfers or quashes.

qa.q: What is the status of the right to property in India today?
qa.a: It is a constitutional/legal right, not a Fundamental Right
qa.e: The 44th Amendment (1978) removed it from Part III; it is now under Article 300A.

qa.q: Which statement about the National Human Rights Commission is correct?
qa.a: It inquires into complaints of rights violations and makes recommendations, but cannot punish the guilty itself
qa.e: The NHRC is a statutory body (1993) with inquiry and recommendatory powers.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A citizen can directly approach the Supreme Court if a Fundamental Right is violated. Reason (R): Article 32 itself is a Fundamental Right.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; because the remedy is itself a Fundamental Right, direct access to the Supreme Court is guaranteed.

qa.q: What does it mean that the Directive Principles are 'non-justiciable'?
qa.a: They cannot be enforced by courts
qa.e: Non-justiciable means no court can compel the state to implement them.

qa.q: Which of the following is a Directive Principle and not a Fundamental Right?
qa.a: Equal pay for equal work for both men and women
qa.e: Equal pay is a DPSP; the others are Fundamental Rights.

qa.q: Which of these is listed among the policies in the Directive Principles?
qa.a: Uniform civil code
qa.e: UCC is a DPSP policy.

qa.q: Which law is an example of implementing a Directive Principle?
qa.a: MGNREGA (2005), which gave rural households guaranteed wage employment
qa.e: The right to work is a DPSP; MGNREGA (2005) gave it legal form. It was replaced in 2025 by a new rural employment guarantee law, which continues the same idea.

qa.q: Why were the DPSPs made non-justiciable?
qa.a: The newly independent state lacked resources to implement all of them at once
qa.e: They were goals to be achieved progressively as resources allowed.

qa.q: Which is a goal of the Directive Principles?
qa.a: Promotion of international peace
qa.e: International peace is among the DPSP goals.

qa.q: Assertion (A): DPSPs are called 'fundamental in the governance of the country'. Reason (R): Courts can punish governments that fail to implement DPSPs.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false, because DPSPs are non-justiciable and courts cannot enforce them.

qa.q: Promotion of village panchayats, a Directive Principle, was given constitutional status by
qa.a: the 73rd Amendment
qa.e: The 73rd Amendment (1992) created the constitutional framework for panchayats.

qa.q: Fundamental Duties were added to the Constitution by which amendment?
qa.a: 42nd Amendment (1976)
qa.e: The 42nd Amendment inserted Article 51A.

qa.q: In which Article are Fundamental Duties listed?
qa.a: Article 51A
qa.e: Article 51A in Part IVA lists the duties.

qa.q: Which of the following is a Fundamental Duty?
qa.a: To develop the scientific temper, humanism and spirit of inquiry
qa.e: Scientific temper is listed in Article 51A; compulsory voting is not.

qa.q: What is the key difference between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles?
qa.a: Fundamental Rights are enforceable by courts while Directive Principles are not
qa.e: Justiciability is the main difference; FR restrain the state, DPSP guide it.

qa.q: Which right was at the centre of the conflict between FR and DPSP in the early decades?
qa.a: Right to property
qa.e: Land reforms based on DPSP clashed with the then Fundamental Right to property.

qa.q: Fundamental Rights mainly ___ the state, while Directive Principles ___ the state.
qa.a: restrain; direct
qa.e: FR are limits; DPSP are positive instructions.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Fundamental Duties are not enforceable by courts. Reason (R): They were added only by the 42nd Amendment and not by the original Constitution.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true, but being added later is not why they are unenforceable; their nature as moral obligations is.

qa.q: A survey asks students to classify 'protection against arbitrary arrest'. Where does it belong?
qa.a: Fundamental Right
qa.e: It is part of Article 22 in Part III.

qa.q: In which form of democracy do citizens themselves take part in day-to-day decision-making?
qa.a: Direct democracy
qa.e: In direct democracy citizens decide directly; in indirect democracy they elect representatives.

qa.q: Why is indirect democracy necessary in modern states like India?
qa.a: Because the population and area are too large for all citizens to decide everything directly
qa.e: Scale makes direct participation in every decision impossible.

qa.q: Which of these is an example of direct democracy in India?
qa.a: A Gram Sabha meeting of all adult voters of a village
qa.e: In a Gram Sabha every adult voter can directly participate.

qa.q: Which of the following is NOT a question that a constitution's election rules usually answer?
qa.a: Which party's manifesto is best
qa.e: The Constitution sets neutral rules, not judgments on manifestos.

qa.q: What is the main purpose of putting basic election rules in the Constitution instead of ordinary law?
qa.a: To protect the electoral process from being changed easily by the party in power
qa.e: Constitutional rules are harder to change, which protects fairness.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Elections are central to representative democracy. Reason (R): Through elections, people choose representatives and can hold them accountable.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; choosing and removing representatives is why elections are central.

qa.q: In ancient Greek city-states, citizens met together to make laws. This was
qa.a: direct democracy
qa.e: Citizens deciding in person is direct democracy.

qa.q: A system in which representatives are elected and run the government on behalf of citizens is called
qa.a: representative or indirect democracy
qa.e: Elected representatives acting for the people define indirect democracy.

qa.q: Under FPTP, which candidate wins in a constituency?
qa.a: The candidate who gets more votes than any other candidate
qa.e: FPTP is a plurality system; the highest vote-getter wins even without a majority.

qa.q: A wins 41%, B 39%, C 20% of votes in a constituency. What percentage of voters did NOT vote for the winner?
qa.e: 100 − 41 = 59% of voters chose someone else.

qa.q: Why is FPTP called a 'winner takes all' system?
qa.a: Only the top candidate gets the seat; votes for others do not translate into any representation
qa.e: Votes for losing candidates are wasted in seat terms.

qa.q: Which was a reason the Constitution makers chose FPTP for India?
qa.a: It is simple and easy to understand for voters
qa.e: Simplicity, voter-candidate link and stability favoured FPTP.

qa.q: In 1984 the Congress won less than half the votes but more than three-fourths of the Lok Sabha seats. This shows that
qa.a: FPTP can magnify a party's lead into a much larger share of seats
qa.e: FPTP often over-rewards the leading party.

qa.q: How does FPTP tend to shape party competition?
qa.a: It encourages broad coalitions of social groups within parties and competition between two main parties or alliances
qa.e: Narrow parties rarely win seats, so parties broaden their base or form alliances.

qa.q: Assertion (A): FPTP was considered suitable for a parliamentary system in India. Reason (R): FPTP tends to give the largest party or coalition a clear majority, producing a stable government.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; stability through clear majorities was a key reason for preferring FPTP.

qa.q: In a constituency of 2,00,000 voters who all voted, P gets 70,000, Q gets 65,000 and R gets 65,000 votes. What is the winner's vote share?
Under Proportional Representation, how are seats distributed?
qa.a: In proportion to the share of votes each party receives
qa.e: PR aims to match seat share with vote share.

qa.q: In which countries is the whole country treated as a single constituency for PR?
qa.a: Israel and the Netherlands
qa.e: Israel and the Netherlands elect their legislatures from one national constituency.

qa.q: Which election in India uses the Single Transferable Vote?
qa.a: Election of Rajya Sabha members
qa.e: Rajya Sabha (and President, Vice-President, Legislative Councils) use STV; direct elections use FPTP.

qa.q: A State Assembly of 140 MLAs elects 6 Rajya Sabha members. What is the STV quota?
In an election under PR with 200 seats, Party X gets 35% of votes. How many seats should it get?
qa.e: 35% of 200 = 70 seats.

qa.q: Five constituencies vote identically: A 40%, B 35%, C 25%. Under FPTP, how many of the 5 seats does A win?
qa.e: A has the most votes in every constituency, so it wins all 5 seats under FPTP even though it has only 40% of votes.

qa.q: Which is a feature of PR but NOT of FPTP?
qa.a: More than one representative may be elected from a constituency
qa.e: PR uses multi-member constituencies.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The President of India is elected by First Past the Post. Reason (R): The Lok Sabha is elected using First Past the Post.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: the President is elected by an electoral college using STV. R is true: Lok Sabha seats are filled by FPTP.

qa.q: In a constituency reserved for Scheduled Castes, who is eligible to vote?
qa.a: All registered voters of that constituency
qa.e: Reservation restricts who can contest, not who can vote.

qa.q: Who can contest from a seat reserved for Scheduled Tribes?
qa.a: Only candidates belonging to the Scheduled Tribes
qa.e: Only ST candidates may contest an ST-reserved seat.

qa.q: Which body decides which constituencies will be reserved?
qa.a: The Delimitation Commission
qa.e: The Delimitation Commission draws boundaries and identifies reserved seats.

qa.q: How is the system of reserved constituencies different from a separate electorate?
qa.a: In reserved constituencies all voters vote; in a separate electorate only members of the group vote
qa.e: India rejected separate electorates and chose joint electorates with reserved seats.

qa.q: The Delimitation Commission is appointed by
qa.a: the President of India
qa.e: The President appoints it; it works with the Election Commission.

qa.q: What does the Constitution (106th Amendment) Act, 2023 provide?
qa.a: One-third of seats in the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies reserved for women
qa.e: It reserves one-third of seats for women, effective after census and delimitation.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Reserved constituencies ensure representation of SC and ST communities. Reason (R): Only members of these communities can vote in reserved constituencies.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false: all voters vote; only candidates must belong to the reserved community.

qa.q: Why does a winning candidate in a reserved constituency need support from many communities?
qa.a: Because all voters of the constituency, including those from other communities, take part in the vote
qa.e: Joint electorates make winners accountable to everyone in the constituency.

qa.q: What is the minimum age to vote in India today?
qa.a: 18 years
qa.e: The 61st Amendment lowered the voting age from 21 to 18.

qa.q: What is the minimum age to contest a Lok Sabha election?
qa.a: 25 years
qa.e: Lok Sabha and Assembly candidates must be at least 25.

qa.q: Which Article provides for the Election Commission of India?
qa.a: Article 324
qa.e: Article 324 vests superintendence, direction and control of elections in the EC.

qa.q: How can the Chief Election Commissioner be removed?
qa.a: In the same manner as a judge of the Supreme Court, by a special majority in both Houses
qa.e: This protects the CEC's independence.

qa.q: Since when has the Election Commission of India been a multi-member body continuously?
qa.e: After a brief experiment in 1989–90, it became multi-member again in 1993 and has remained so.

qa.q: Which statement about qualifications to contest elections in India is correct?
qa.a: There is no minimum educational qualification for contesting
qa.e: Universal franchise extends to the right to contest, subject to age and certain disqualifications.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The Election Commission of India is an independent body. Reason (R): The CEC has security of tenure and can be removed only through a difficult procedure.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; security of tenure is one of the main sources of the EC's independence.

qa.q: Which amendment lowered the voting age from 21 to 18?
qa.a: 61st Amendment
qa.e: The 61st Amendment (1988) lowered the voting age.

qa.q: Which of the following is a function of the Election Commission of India?
qa.a: Allotting election symbols to political parties
qa.e: Symbol allotment and party recognition are EC functions.

qa.q: Which body conducts elections to municipalities and panchayats?
qa.a: The State Election Commission
qa.e: Local body elections are conducted by State Election Commissions.

qa.q: The set of rules that guides the behaviour of parties and candidates once elections are announced is called the
qa.a: Model Code of Conduct
qa.e: The EC enforces the Model Code of Conduct during elections.

qa.q: If voting in a polling booth is marred by rigging, the Election Commission can
qa.a: order a re-poll in that booth
qa.e: The EC can order re-polls where polling was unfair.

qa.q: Since which Lok Sabha election have EVMs been used in all constituencies?
qa.e: The 2004 Lok Sabha election was the first fully conducted on EVMs.

qa.q: Who controls government officers deployed on election duty during an election?
qa.a: The Election Commission
qa.e: Election-duty officials work under EC control, which helps fairness.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The Election Commission can prepare and update the electoral rolls. Reason (R): An accurate voters' list is essential for free and fair elections.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the importance of accurate rolls is why the EC supervises them.

qa.q: Which is the best example of the EC ensuring a level playing field?
qa.a: Stopping a minister from announcing new schemes after elections are declared
qa.e: Under the Model Code, the government cannot announce new schemes to influence voters.

qa.q: About 45% of voters turned out in India's first general election (1951–52); in 2019 Lok Sabha turnout reached a record of about 67%. What broad trend does this show?
qa.a: Voter participation has broadly grown over the decades
qa.e: A rise from about 45% to about 67% shows that more and more registered voters, including women and rural voters, have taken part over the decades.

qa.q: Which reform aims to make seats better reflect votes?
qa.a: Shifting from FPTP to a PR or mixed system
qa.e: PR or mixed systems align seats with vote shares.

qa.q: Candidates must declare their criminal cases and assets in an affidavit. This reform targets
qa.a: criminalisation and lack of transparency in politics
qa.e: Disclosure lets voters know a candidate's background.

qa.q: State funding of elections is proposed mainly to
qa.a: reduce the influence of money power on elections
qa.e: Public funding aims to reduce dependence on private money.

qa.q: A candidate's speech asks people to vote for him because he belongs to their caste. Which reform proposal would address this?
qa.a: A complete ban on caste and religious appeals in campaigns
qa.e: Banning such appeals targets divisive campaigning.

qa.q: Which country is often cited as an example of a mixed electoral system?
qa.a: Germany
qa.e: Germany combines constituency seats with PR list seats.

qa.q: Case: In a state election, Party P wins 70% of seats with 42% of votes. A commentator proposes a reform. Which is most relevant?
qa.a: Moving towards a PR or mixed system
qa.e: The gap between votes and seats is an FPTP effect; PR addresses it.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A law to regulate the functioning of political parties has been suggested as an electoral reform. Reason (R): Parties play a central role in elections and their internal working affects democracy.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the importance of parties is why their regulation is proposed.

qa.q: Which reform proposal relates to gender representation?
qa.a: Reserving one-third of seats in legislatures for women
qa.e: Women's reservation aims to increase women's representation.

qa.q: What is the primary function of the executive?
qa.a: Implementing laws and policies
qa.e: The executive carries out laws; the legislature makes them and the judiciary interprets them.

qa.q: Which of the following is part of the permanent executive?
qa.a: A District Collector from the IAS
qa.e: Civil servants form the permanent executive; ministers are the political executive.

qa.q: In a presidential system, the President is
qa.a: head of both the state and the government
qa.e: In a presidential system, one person heads state and government.

qa.q: Which country has a semi-presidential system?
qa.a: France
qa.e: France has a powerful President and a PM; the USA is presidential, the UK and Japan are parliamentary.

qa.q: In a parliamentary system, the real executive is
qa.a: the Prime Minister and the Council of Ministers
qa.e: The PM-led ministry is the real executive and answers to the legislature.

qa.q: Which feature distinguishes a parliamentary executive from a presidential one?
qa.a: The executive is responsible to the legislature and can be removed by a no-confidence vote
qa.e: Accountability to the legislature is the hallmark of parliamentary government.

qa.q: Assertion (A): In a semi-presidential system, the President and the Prime Minister may belong to different parties. Reason (R): The President is directly elected while the Prime Minister needs the support of the legislature, which may be controlled by another party.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; separate sources of power explain why they can come from different parties.

qa.q: Germany and Japan are examples of which type of executive?
qa.a: Parliamentary
qa.e: Both have a head of government responsible to parliament.

qa.q: Who elects the President of India?
qa.a: An electoral college of elected members of both Houses of Parliament and elected members of State Legislative Assemblies
qa.e: The President is indirectly elected by this electoral college using STV.

qa.q: On what ground can the President of India be impeached?
qa.a: Violation of the Constitution
qa.e: Article 61 allows impeachment only for violation of the Constitution.

qa.q: Why is the Indian President described as a 'nominal' executive?
qa.a: Because real executive power is exercised by the Council of Ministers headed by the PM
qa.e: Powers are formally vested in the President but exercised on ministerial advice.

qa.q: Which was a reason for India choosing the parliamentary system?
qa.a: To keep the executive accountable to elected representatives
qa.e: Accountability to the legislature was a key reason.

qa.q: What is the term of office of the President of India?
qa.a: 5 years
qa.e: The President holds office for five years.

qa.q: What is the minimum age to be elected President of India?
qa.a: 35 years
qa.e: A candidate for President must be at least 35.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The President of India cannot claim a personal popular mandate against the elected government. Reason (R): The President is elected indirectly rather than directly by the people.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; indirect election is why the President lacks a separate direct mandate.

qa.q: Which voting method is used in the election of the President of India?
qa.a: Single Transferable Vote (proportional representation)
qa.e: STV is used for the President's election.

qa.q: Under Article 74(1), the President must act
qa.a: in accordance with the advice of the Council of Ministers
qa.e: Article 74(1) binds the President to ministerial advice.

qa.q: How many times can the President ask the Council of Ministers to reconsider its advice?
qa.a: Once
qa.e: The President may return advice once; after reconsideration, it is binding.

qa.q: Which type of bill can the President NOT return for reconsideration?
qa.a: A money bill
qa.e: Money bills cannot be returned.

qa.q: What is meant by the President's 'pocket veto'?
qa.a: Keeping a bill pending without signing or returning it, since no time limit is fixed
qa.e: The absence of a deadline allows the President to delay a bill indefinitely.

qa.q: Which bill is the famous example of a pocket veto by a President of India?
qa.a: The Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill, 1986
qa.e: President Zail Singh did not act on this bill.

qa.q: When does the President have real discretion in appointing the Prime Minister?
qa.a: When no party or coalition has a clear majority in the Lok Sabha
qa.e: With a clear majority the choice is obvious; in a hung House the President uses judgment.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The President has the right to be informed of all important decisions of the Council of Ministers. Reason (R): The Prime Minister is required to communicate such decisions and information to the President.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the PM's duty to communicate is what gives the President this right.

qa.q: Which of these is a military power of the President?
qa.a: Supreme Command of the defence forces
qa.e: The President is Supreme Commander, though decisions are taken on ministerial advice.

qa.q: Who is the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha?
qa.a: The Vice-President
qa.e: The Vice-President presides over the Rajya Sabha.

qa.q: Who elects the Vice-President of India?
qa.a: Members of both Houses of Parliament
qa.e: Unlike the President, MLAs do not vote for the Vice-President.

qa.q: A person who is not a member of Parliament is appointed a minister. Within how many months must she become an MP?
qa.a: 6 months
qa.e: The limit is six months.

qa.q: A State Assembly has 200 members. Under the 91st Amendment, what is the maximum size of its Council of Ministers, including the Chief Minister?
Which amendment limited the size of the Council of Ministers to 15% of the Lok Sabha's membership?
qa.a: 91st Amendment (2003)
qa.e: The 91st Amendment introduced the cap.

qa.q: 'Collective responsibility' means that
qa.a: the whole Council of Ministers is responsible to the Lok Sabha and stands or falls together
qa.e: If the Lok Sabha loses confidence, the entire ministry resigns.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A government falls if the Lok Sabha passes a no-confidence motion against it. Reason (R): The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; collective responsibility is why a no-confidence vote brings down the whole ministry.

qa.q: The Lok Sabha has 543 members. Which number is the maximum size of the Union Council of Ministers?
qa.e: 15% of 543 = 81.45; as the size cannot exceed 15%, the maximum is 81.

qa.q: Who is the nominal executive head of a State?
qa.a: The Governor
qa.e: The Governor is the nominal head; the CM-led ministry is the real executive.

qa.q: Who appoints the Governor of a State?
qa.a: The President
qa.e: Governors are appointed by the President.

qa.q: Which rank of minister is usually in charge of a major ministry and part of the inner decision-making body?
qa.a: Cabinet Minister
qa.e: Cabinet Ministers head major ministries and form the Cabinet.

qa.q: How does coalition politics generally affect the power of the Prime Minister?
qa.a: It limits the PM's power, since allies must be consulted and accommodated
qa.e: Coalition partners bargain for ministries and policies.

qa.q: Who leads the real executive in a State?
qa.a: The Chief Minister with the Council of Ministers
qa.e: The CM-led ministry, responsible to the Assembly, is the real executive.

qa.q: What binds every minister to defend Cabinet decisions in public even if they disagreed in private?
qa.a: Collective responsibility
qa.e: Ministers swim or sink together; dissent stays inside the Cabinet.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A Prime Minister heading a single-party majority usually enjoys more authority than one heading a coalition. Reason (R): In a coalition, allies can withdraw support and bring down the government.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the threat of allies withdrawing is why coalition PMs have less authority.

qa.q: A Minister of State who holds independent charge
qa.a: heads a ministry without a Cabinet Minister above them
qa.e: Independent charge means the minister runs the ministry on their own, though below Cabinet rank.

qa.q: The bureaucracy is called the 'permanent executive' because
qa.a: civil servants remain in office regardless of changes in government
qa.e: Ministers change with elections; civil servants continue.

qa.q: Which body recruits officers for the All India Services such as the IAS and IPS?
qa.a: Union Public Service Commission
qa.e: The UPSC conducts recruitment for All India and central services.

qa.q: What does 'political neutrality' of the civil service mean?
qa.a: Civil servants serve any elected government impartially without supporting a party
qa.e: Neutrality means impartial service to whichever government is in power.

qa.q: Which is a common criticism of the bureaucracy?
qa.a: Red tape and insensitivity to ordinary citizens
qa.e: Delays, rigidity and insensitivity are frequent complaints.

qa.q: Which law has helped citizens hold the bureaucracy accountable by giving access to government information?
qa.a: Right to Information Act, 2005
qa.e: RTI gives citizens a legal right to information.

qa.q: Why are reservations provided in recruitment to the civil services?
qa.a: To make the bureaucracy more representative of society and include disadvantaged groups
qa.e: Representation of SC, ST and OBC ensures social diversity in administration.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Ministers depend heavily on civil servants. Reason (R): Civil servants have expertise, experience and continuity in administration.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; their expertise and continuity explain why ministers rely on them.

qa.q: Which pair is correctly matched?
qa.a: District Collector — permanent executive
qa.e: Collectors are civil servants; ministers are political executive.

qa.q: Which of these is the constituent function of Parliament?
qa.a: Amending the Constitution
qa.e: Constituent power is the power to amend the Constitution.

qa.q: Impeachment of the President by Parliament is an example of its
qa.a: judicial function
qa.e: Removal of high officials is a quasi-judicial function of Parliament.

qa.q: Why is Parliament called the most representative organ of government?
qa.a: It has members elected from all regions and social groups who voice different views
qa.e: Diverse elected members make it the main forum of representation.

qa.q: Which statement best explains the 'decline of legislatures'?
qa.a: Power has shifted towards the executive due to strong cabinets and party discipline
qa.e: Executive dominance and party control limit legislative independence.

qa.q: Which is the financial function of Parliament?
qa.a: Approving taxes and government expenditure
qa.e: No tax or spending is valid without Parliament's approval.

qa.q: Electing the Vice-President is an example of Parliament's
qa.a: electoral function
qa.e: Parliament's members elect the Vice-President.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The legislature is central to representative democracy. Reason (R): It makes laws, debates public issues and holds the executive accountable on behalf of the people.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; these roles performed on the people's behalf are why it is central.

qa.q: Which of the following is NOT a function of Parliament?
qa.a: Issuing writs for enforcement of Fundamental Rights
qa.e: Writs are issued by the Supreme Court and High Courts.

qa.q: How are members of the Rajya Sabha elected?
qa.a: Indirectly, by elected members of the State Legislative Assemblies
qa.e: MLAs elect Rajya Sabha members using STV.

qa.q: Why is the Rajya Sabha called a 'permanent House'?
qa.a: It is never dissolved; one-third of its members retire every two years
qa.e: Staggered terms mean the House continues indefinitely.

qa.q: How many members can the President nominate to the Rajya Sabha?
qa.e: Twelve members with special knowledge of literature, science, art and social service.

qa.q: How does representation in the Rajya Sabha differ from the US Senate?
qa.a: India gives States seats based on population, while the USA gives every state two seats
qa.e: India follows unequal (population-based) representation; the USA follows equal representation.

qa.q: What is the term of a Rajya Sabha member?
qa.a: 6 years
qa.e: Rajya Sabha members serve six-year terms.

qa.q: Which of the following can be dissolved before completing its term?
qa.a: Lok Sabha
qa.e: The Lok Sabha can be dissolved; the Rajya Sabha cannot.

qa.q: Assertion (A): India has a bicameral Parliament. Reason (R): The Lok Sabha is presided over by the Speaker.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true, but who presides over the Lok Sabha does not explain why Parliament has two Houses; the need to represent both people and States does.

qa.q: Nominated members of the Rajya Sabha are chosen from people with special knowledge or experience in
qa.a: literature, science, art and social service
qa.e: These four fields are listed in the Constitution.

qa.q: Most States have a unicameral legislature. Which of these States has a bicameral legislature, with a Legislative Council as well as a Legislative Assembly?
qa.a: Bihar
qa.e: Bihar is one of the few States (with Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh and Telangana) that has a Legislative Council. Kerala, Punjab and Gujarat have only an Assembly.

qa.q: Within how many days must the Rajya Sabha return a money bill?
qa.a: 14 days
qa.e: The Rajya Sabha has 14 days to make recommendations.

qa.q: Who decides whether a bill is a money bill?
qa.a: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha
qa.e: The Speaker certifies money bills.

qa.q: Which power does the Lok Sabha have but the Rajya Sabha does not?
qa.a: Removing the Council of Ministers by a no-confidence motion
qa.e: Ministers are responsible only to the Lok Sabha.

qa.q: Under Article 249, the Rajya Sabha can
qa.a: allow Parliament to make laws on a State List subject in the national interest
qa.e: This special power protects State interests through the House of States.

qa.q: What majority does a Rajya Sabha resolution under Article 249 need?
qa.a: Two-thirds of the members present and voting
qa.e: Article 249 requires a two-thirds resolution.

qa.q: Why is the Lok Sabha considered more powerful than the Rajya Sabha?
qa.a: It is directly elected and controls money bills and the ministry
qa.e: Direct election, control of finance and of the ministry give it more power.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The Rajya Sabha has special powers to protect the interests of States. Reason (R): It is the House that represents the States in Parliament.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; representing States is why it has powers like Article 249 and creating All India Services.

qa.q: For ordinary (non-money) bills, what is the position of the two Houses?
qa.a: Both Houses have equal powers, and a joint sitting can resolve a deadlock
qa.e: Non-money bills need passage by both Houses.

qa.q: A bill introduced by an MP who is not a minister is called a
qa.a: private member's bill
qa.e: Private members' bills come from MPs who are not ministers.

qa.q: In which House can a money bill be introduced?
qa.a: Only in the Lok Sabha
qa.e: Money bills originate only in the Lok Sabha.

qa.q: Who presides over a joint sitting of the two Houses?
qa.a: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha
qa.e: The Speaker presides over joint sittings.

qa.q: When does a bill become an Act?
qa.a: After it is passed by both Houses and receives the President's assent
qa.e: Assent is the final step.

qa.q: Why is a joint sitting held?
qa.a: To resolve a deadlock between the two Houses over an ordinary bill
qa.e: Joint sittings resolve disagreements on non-money bills.

qa.q: What usually happens at the committee stage of a bill?
qa.a: Members examine the bill in detail and may suggest changes
qa.e: Committees scrutinise bills closely.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The Rajya Sabha cannot block a money bill permanently. Reason (R): A money bill is deemed passed by both Houses if the Rajya Sabha does not return it within 14 days.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the 14-day deeming rule is exactly why it cannot block the bill.

qa.q: Which is the correct order of stages for a bill in a House?
qa.a: Introduction → committee → clause-by-clause debate → final vote
qa.e: A bill is introduced, studied, debated in detail and then voted on.

qa.q: The first hour of a sitting, when MPs ask ministers questions, is called
qa.a: Question Hour
qa.e: Question Hour is usually the first hour of a sitting.

qa.q: Which of the following is the 'ultimate' parliamentary weapon against the executive?
qa.a: No-confidence motion
qa.e: Passing it forces the entire government to resign.

qa.q: Who audits the accounts of the Union government and reports to Parliament?
qa.a: The Comptroller and Auditor General
qa.e: The CAG audits government spending; reports go to Parliament.

qa.q: The Public Accounts Committee examines
qa.a: the reports of the Comptroller and Auditor General
qa.e: The PAC scrutinises CAG audit reports.

qa.q: What is Zero Hour?
qa.a: Time when members raise urgent issues, an Indian parliamentary innovation
qa.e: Zero Hour follows Question Hour and allows urgent matters to be raised.

qa.q: Why may parliamentary control over the executive be weak when the ruling party has a large majority?
qa.a: Party discipline ensures government bills and motions pass easily
qa.e: Large majorities plus discipline reduce effective control.

qa.q: Assertion (A): An adjournment motion is a means of parliamentary control. Reason (R): It allows the House to set aside its normal business to discuss a definite matter of urgent public importance.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; discussing urgent failures of government is how it acts as control.

qa.q: A government needs Parliament to pass its bills and its budget. This gives Parliament control through
qa.a: approval and ratification
qa.e: Without Parliament's approval, the executive's plans cannot become law.

qa.q: What is the main advantage of parliamentary committees?
qa.a: They allow detailed, expert and less partisan scrutiny of bills and government work
qa.e: Committees study matters in depth on behalf of the House.

qa.q: Which committee is set up with members of both Houses to examine a bill or investigate irregularities?
qa.a: Joint Parliamentary Committee
qa.e: JPCs include members of both Houses.

qa.q: The anti-defection law was introduced by which amendment?
qa.a: 52nd Amendment (1985)
qa.e: The 52nd Amendment added the Tenth Schedule.

qa.q: Who decides whether a member is disqualified under the anti-defection law?
qa.a: The presiding officer of the House
qa.e: The Speaker/Chairman decides disqualification petitions.

qa.q: A member of the Lok Sabha cannot be sued in court for a speech made in the House. This is an example of
qa.a: parliamentary privilege
qa.e: Freedom of speech in the House is a parliamentary privilege.

qa.q: What did the 91st Amendment (2003) change in the anti-defection law?
qa.a: It removed the exception that protected a 'split' by one-third of a party's members
qa.e: After 2003, a split is no longer a defence; only a merger supported by two-thirds is protected.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Department-related standing committees improve the quality of legislation. Reason (R): They examine bills and ministries' work in detail and include members from different parties.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; detailed, cross-party scrutiny is why they improve laws.

qa.q: Which officer is the final authority on the conduct of business in the Lok Sabha?
qa.a: The Speaker
qa.e: The Speaker regulates proceedings and decides points of order.

qa.q: What is the retirement age of a Supreme Court judge?
qa.a: 65 years
qa.e: Supreme Court judges retire at 65; High Court judges at 62.

qa.q: Which of the following is a safeguard of judicial independence?
qa.a: Judges' salaries are not subject to the vote of the legislature
qa.e: Financial independence keeps judges free from pressure.

qa.q: Independence of the judiciary means
qa.a: the legislature and executive must not interfere with the judiciary's functioning
qa.e: Independence is freedom from interference, not freedom from the Constitution.

qa.q: To whom is the independent judiciary ultimately accountable?
qa.a: To the Constitution, democratic traditions and the people
qa.e: Courts derive authority from and answer to the Constitution.

qa.q: What is the retirement age of a High Court judge?
qa.a: 62 years
qa.e: High Court judges retire at 62.

qa.q: Why can the conduct of judges not be discussed in the legislature except during removal proceedings?
qa.a: To protect judges from pressure and political attack
qa.e: This shields judges' independence; removal has its own procedure.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The judiciary in India is independent. Reason (R): Judges cannot be removed easily and their salaries are not voted on by the legislature.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; secure tenure and finances are major reasons for independence.

qa.q: The main role of the judiciary in a democracy includes all of these EXCEPT
qa.a: making the annual budget
qa.e: The budget is prepared by the executive and passed by the legislature.

qa.q: On what grounds can a Supreme Court judge be removed?
qa.a: Proven misbehaviour or incapacity
qa.e: The Constitution allows removal only for proven misbehaviour or incapacity.

qa.q: What majority is required in each House to remove a judge?
qa.a: A majority of total membership and two-thirds of members present and voting
qa.e: This special majority makes removal very difficult.

qa.q: In 1973, the convention of appointing the senior-most judge as Chief Justice was broken when ___ was appointed CJI.
qa.a: Justice A.N. Ray
qa.e: A.N. Ray was appointed over three senior judges.

qa.q: The 'collegium' for Supreme Court appointments consists of
qa.a: the Chief Justice of India and the four senior-most Supreme Court judges
qa.e: The collegium is a body of senior judges.

qa.q: The removal motion against Justice V. Ramaswami
qa.a: failed in Parliament
qa.e: It failed to obtain the required special majority.

qa.q: Who formally appoints judges of the Supreme Court?
qa.a: The President
qa.e: Appointment is made by the President, with recommendations from the collegium.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Very few judges have faced removal proceedings in India. Reason (R): The removal procedure requires a special majority in both Houses and proof of misbehaviour or incapacity.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the difficulty of the procedure explains why it is rarely used.

qa.q: In the Lok Sabha of 543 members, 420 are present and voting on a removal motion. How many votes are needed to satisfy the two-thirds condition?
qa.e: 2/3 × 420 = 280. (This also exceeds 272, the majority of total membership.)

qa.q: What does 'single integrated judicial system' mean in India?
qa.a: One hierarchy of courts with the Supreme Court at the top for the whole country
qa.e: India has one unified hierarchy, unlike the USA.

qa.q: Whose decisions are binding on all courts in India?
qa.a: The Supreme Court
qa.e: The Supreme Court's law is binding throughout India.

qa.q: Which court supervises and controls subordinate courts in a State?
qa.a: The High Court
qa.e: High Courts exercise control over subordinate courts.

qa.q: Which court usually deals with cases arising in a district?
qa.a: The District Court
qa.e: District Courts handle cases in their district.

qa.q: A litigant unhappy with a High Court judgment can appeal to
qa.a: the Supreme Court
qa.e: Appeals from High Courts go to the Supreme Court.

qa.q: Why is a single integrated judiciary useful for a diverse country like India?
qa.a: It ensures a uniform interpretation of laws across the country
qa.e: Uniform interpretation strengthens national legal unity.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A judgment of a High Court is binding on all courts throughout India. Reason (R): The Supreme Court is at the top of a single integrated judicial system.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: a High Court binds courts within its own jurisdiction; only the Supreme Court's law binds all courts. R is true.

qa.q: Which is the correct order from lowest to highest?
qa.a: Subordinate court → District Court → High Court → Supreme Court
qa.e: Appeals move upward from subordinate courts to the Supreme Court.

qa.q: A dispute between two States is filed directly in the Supreme Court. This is its
qa.a: original jurisdiction
qa.e: Federal disputes go directly to the Supreme Court.

qa.q: Under which Article can the President seek the advice of the Supreme Court?
qa.a: Article 143
qa.e: Article 143 provides advisory jurisdiction.

qa.q: Is the advice given by the Supreme Court under advisory jurisdiction binding on the President?
qa.a: No, it is not binding
qa.e: The advice is an opinion; the President is not bound by it.

qa.q: Which Article allows a person to directly move the Supreme Court for enforcement of Fundamental Rights?
qa.a: Article 32
qa.e: Article 32 provides writ jurisdiction of the Supreme Court.

qa.q: Under Article 136, the Supreme Court can
qa.a: grant special leave to appeal against any judgment of any court in India
qa.e: Article 136 is a wide discretionary appellate power.

qa.q: Hearing an appeal against a High Court verdict in a criminal case is the Supreme Court's
qa.a: appellate jurisdiction
qa.e: Appeals from High Courts fall under appellate jurisdiction.

qa.q: Assertion (A): High Courts have a wider writ jurisdiction than the Supreme Court. Reason (R): Under Article 226, High Courts can issue writs for Fundamental Rights and also for other legal purposes.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the 'other purposes' clause is why High Court writ jurisdiction is wider.

qa.q: Which power allows the Supreme Court to pass any order needed to do 'complete justice' in a case?
qa.a: Article 142
qa.e: Article 142 gives this extraordinary power.

qa.q: What is 'locus standi'?
qa.a: The right of a person to approach a court, traditionally only if personally affected
qa.e: PIL relaxed the traditional rule of locus standi.

qa.q: Public Interest Litigation allows
qa.a: a person or group to approach the court on behalf of others whose rights are violated
qa.e: PIL widens access to courts for public causes.

qa.q: The Hussainara Khatoon case (1979) dealt with
qa.a: undertrial prisoners in Bihar jails
qa.e: It highlighted the long detention of undertrials.

qa.q: Which is a criticism of judicial activism?
qa.a: It can blur the separation of powers between the organs of government
qa.e: Courts may end up doing executive or legislative work.

qa.q: Which is a positive effect of PIL?
qa.a: It has made courts accessible to the poor and disadvantaged
qa.e: PIL brought the concerns of voiceless groups to courts.

qa.q: When did PIL emerge in India?
qa.a: In the late 1970s and early 1980s
qa.e: Landmark PIL cases began around 1979–80.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Judicial activism has increased the accountability of the executive. Reason (R): Through PIL, courts have directed government agencies to perform their duties.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; court directions to agencies are why accountability increased.

qa.q: A court treats a letter from a prisoner describing torture in jail as a petition. This is an example of
qa.a: judicial activism through PIL
qa.e: Accepting letters as petitions was a hallmark of PIL.

qa.q: What is 'judicial review'?
qa.a: The power of courts to examine the constitutionality of laws and strike down those that violate the Constitution
qa.e: Judicial review checks laws against the Constitution.

qa.q: In which case did the Supreme Court hold that Parliament cannot amend Fundamental Rights?
qa.a: Golaknath (1967)
qa.e: Golaknath restricted Parliament's power over Fundamental Rights.

qa.q: What did the Supreme Court decide in Kesavananda Bharati (1973)?
qa.a: Parliament can amend the Constitution but cannot alter its basic structure
qa.e: The basic structure doctrine balances amendment power with core values.

qa.q: Which right was at the centre of early conflicts between Parliament and the judiciary?
qa.a: Right to property
qa.e: Land reforms and property rights sparked these conflicts.

qa.q: The 'basic structure doctrine' acts as a limit on
qa.a: Parliament's power to amend the Constitution
qa.e: It restricts amendments that would destroy core features.

qa.q: Which tension between legislature and judiciary relates to the conduct of judges?
qa.a: Parliament cannot discuss the conduct of judges except during removal proceedings
qa.e: This rule protects judicial independence; courts in turn can punish contempt.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The judiciary is called the guardian of Fundamental Rights. Reason (R): Through writs and judicial review, it can strike down actions and laws that violate rights.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; its remedies and power of review are why it guards rights.

qa.q: A law passed by Parliament is challenged as violating Article 14. Which power will the Court use?
qa.a: Judicial review
qa.e: The Court tests the law's validity against the Constitution.

qa.q: What is the essential feature of federalism?
qa.a: Powers are divided between two or more levels of government by the constitution
qa.e: Constitutional division of powers defines federalism.

qa.q: Why does a federation need an independent judiciary?
qa.a: To settle disputes between the central and State governments
qa.e: Courts act as umpires between levels of government.

qa.q: Which federation broke up in 1991?
qa.a: The Soviet Union
qa.e: The USSR dissolved into 15 independent countries.

qa.q: What does 'federal spirit' mean?
qa.a: Trust, respect and willingness to share power among levels of government
qa.e: Structures work only with a culture of accommodation.

qa.q: Why is federalism considered suitable for diverse societies?
qa.a: It allows regions with different languages and cultures to govern themselves within one country
qa.e: Federalism combines unity with diversity.

qa.q: A constitution that can be changed by the central government alone, without any role for the States, weakens
qa.a: the federal character of the system
qa.e: In a federation, the division of powers should not be changeable by one level alone.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The West Indies Federation did not last long. Reason (R): It lacked a strong sense of shared purpose and mutual trust among its units.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; weak federal spirit explains its failure.

qa.q: Which of the following is NOT a feature of a federation?
qa.a: One level can abolish the other at will
qa.e: In a federation, each level's powers are guaranteed.

qa.q: How does Article 1 describe India?
qa.a: As a Union of States
qa.e: The Constitution uses 'Union of States', not 'federation'.

qa.q: In which Schedule are the Union, State and Concurrent Lists found?
qa.a: Seventh Schedule
qa.e: The Seventh Schedule contains the three lists.

qa.q: Police is a subject in the
qa.a: State List
qa.e: Police and public order are State subjects.

qa.q: Which of these is on the Concurrent List?
qa.a: Education
qa.e: Education is concurrent (moved there by the 42nd Amendment).

qa.q: Who has residuary powers in India?
qa.a: The Union
qa.e: Article 248 gives residuary powers to Parliament.

qa.q: If a State law on a Concurrent List subject conflicts with a Union law, which prevails?
qa.a: The Union law
qa.e: On concurrent subjects, Union law generally prevails in case of conflict.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The Indian Constitution does not use the word 'federation'. Reason (R): Article 1 calls India a 'Union of States'.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; Article 1's wording is exactly why 'federation' is absent.

qa.q: Which subject is in the Union List?
qa.a: Banking
qa.e: Banking is a Union subject; the others are State subjects.

qa.q: Under Article 3, the views of a State legislature on a bill changing its boundaries are
qa.a: sought by the President but not binding on Parliament
qa.e: Parliament can act even if the State disagrees.

qa.q: Which was a reason the Constitution makers created a strong Centre?
qa.a: Concerns about unity after Partition and the integration of princely states
qa.e: Partition and integration made unity a priority.

qa.q: Which body recommends how taxes should be shared between the Centre and States?
qa.a: The Finance Commission
qa.e: Article 280 provides for the Finance Commission.

qa.q: How often is the Finance Commission constituted?
qa.a: Every five years
qa.e: The President appoints it every five years (or earlier if needed).

qa.q: During a national emergency, Indian federalism becomes
qa.a: almost unitary, with the Centre able to legislate on State subjects
qa.e: Emergency powers concentrate authority at the Centre.

qa.q: One sign of a strong Centre is that each State's Governor is appointed by
qa.a: The President of India
qa.e: Governors are appointed by the President, effectively by the Union government.

qa.q: Assertion (A): States in India depend on the Centre for funds. Reason (R): The Centre controls major sources of tax revenue and makes grants to States.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; central control of revenues is why States depend on it.

qa.q: Which feature lets a Governor send a State bill to the President instead of signing it?
qa.a: The power to reserve bills for the President's consideration
qa.e: Governors can reserve State bills for the President.

qa.q: Which Article provides for President's Rule in a State?
qa.a: Article 356
qa.e: Article 356 deals with failure of constitutional machinery in States.

qa.q: What did the Supreme Court hold in S.R. Bommai (1994)?
qa.a: Imposition of President's Rule is subject to judicial review and majority must be tested on the floor
qa.e: Bommai checked the misuse of Article 356.

qa.q: The Sarkaria Commission, set up in 1983, examined
qa.a: Centre–State relations
qa.e: It studied Centre–State relations, including the Governor's role.

qa.q: Why is the role of the Governor often controversial?
qa.a: Because the Governor is appointed by the Centre and may be seen as acting for the ruling party at the Centre
qa.e: Appointment by the Centre leads to charges of partisanship.

qa.q: A State demands control over the officers posted in its administration. This is a demand for
qa.a: administrative autonomy
qa.e: Control over services is an administrative autonomy demand.

qa.q: What changed Centre–State relations significantly from the late 1960s and after 1989?
qa.a: Different parties ruled at the Centre and in States, and coalition politics gave States more voice
qa.e: Party competition and coalitions altered the balance.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Article 356 has been criticised. Reason (R): It has at times been used to dismiss State governments on partisan grounds.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; partisan misuse is why it has been criticised.

qa.q: A State demands a larger share of central taxes. This is a demand for
qa.a: financial autonomy
qa.e: Demands for resources are financial autonomy demands.

qa.q: Which State was carved out of Bihar in 2000?
qa.a: Jharkhand
qa.e: Jharkhand was created from Bihar on 15 November 2000.

qa.q: Telangana was created in
qa.e: Telangana became a State in 2014, carved out of Andhra Pradesh.

qa.q: The States Reorganisation Act, which reorganised many States mainly on linguistic lines, was passed in
qa.e: The Act of 1956 was based on the States Reorganisation Commission's report.

qa.q: The Belgaum (Belagavi) border dispute is between
qa.a: Maharashtra and Karnataka
qa.e: Maharashtra claims Belgaum, which is in Karnataka.

qa.q: Which city is claimed by both Punjab and Haryana and serves as the capital of both?
qa.a: Chandigarh
qa.e: Chandigarh is a Union Territory and the joint capital.

qa.q: The Cauvery water dispute mainly involves
qa.a: Karnataka and Tamil Nadu
qa.e: Kerala and Puducherry are also involved.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Several new States were created in India after 1956. Reason (R): No new State has been created in India since 2000.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false: Telangana was created in 2014.

qa.q: Uttarakhand was carved out of
qa.a: Uttar Pradesh
qa.e: Uttarakhand (initially Uttaranchal) was created from UP in 2000.

qa.q: What is meant by 'asymmetric federalism'?
qa.a: Some States have special provisions in the Constitution because of their particular circumstances
qa.e: Asymmetry means differential treatment to accommodate diversity.

qa.q: Under which Article did Jammu and Kashmir have special status until 2019?
qa.a: Article 370
qa.e: Article 370 gave J&K special status.

qa.q: Into which Union Territories was Jammu and Kashmir reorganised in 2019?
qa.a: Jammu and Kashmir, and Ladakh
qa.e: The 2019 Act created two UTs.

qa.q: Which State has special provisions protecting customary law and land ownership under Article 371A?
qa.a: Nagaland
qa.e: Article 371A applies to Nagaland.

qa.q: Which of these States also has special provisions under the 371 series of Articles?
qa.a: Maharashtra
qa.e: Article 371 includes special provisions for Maharashtra and Gujarat.

qa.q: Why do some States have special provisions?
qa.a: To protect their distinct history, culture, customary laws or development needs
qa.e: Special provisions accommodate diversity within the Union.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Indian federalism is described as accommodating diversity. Reason (R): It makes special provisions for certain States to protect their particular identities and needs.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; special provisions are a key way diversity is accommodated.

qa.q: A student says Article 371 applies only to the North-East. What is the correct position?
qa.a: It also covers other States such as Maharashtra, Gujarat, Goa and Karnataka
qa.e: The 371-series covers many States across India.

qa.q: What is local government?
qa.a: Government at the village, district, town or city level, closest to the people
qa.e: Local bodies like panchayats and municipalities are closest to citizens.

qa.q: What is 'democratic decentralisation'?
qa.a: Transferring powers and resources from higher levels to local elected bodies
qa.e: Decentralisation spreads power downward to elected local bodies.

qa.q: Which is a key benefit of local government?
qa.a: Local people can participate directly and use local knowledge in decisions
qa.e: Participation and local knowledge improve decisions.
