qa.q: Which matter is most suitable for a local government?
qa.a: Maintaining village drains and street lights
qa.e: Local bodies handle local everyday services.

qa.q: Why are problems often solved faster at the local level?
qa.a: Decision-makers are close to the problem and know local conditions
qa.e: Proximity and knowledge speed up decisions.

qa.q: A gram sabha discusses and settles a dispute over common land. This shows that local democracy
qa.a: can resolve conflicts using local participation and knowledge
qa.e: Local institutions can settle local disputes.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Local government strengthens democracy. Reason (R): It allows ordinary citizens to participate in decisions that affect their daily lives.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; participation is exactly how it strengthens democracy.

qa.q: Which pair of local bodies is correct?
qa.a: Panchayats in rural areas; municipalities in urban areas
qa.e: Panchayats are rural; municipalities are urban local bodies.

qa.q: Who is associated with the resolution of 1882 promoting local self-government in British India?
qa.a: Lord Ripon
qa.e: Lord Ripon's 1882 resolution is a milestone in local self-government.

qa.q: Which Article of the Constitution directs the State to organise village panchayats?
qa.a: Article 40
qa.e: Article 40 is a Directive Principle on panchayats.

qa.q: Which committee (1957) recommended a three-tier panchayati raj system?
qa.a: Balwantrai Mehta Committee
qa.e: The Balwantrai Mehta Committee recommended the three-tier system.

qa.q: Gandhi's vision of self-reliant villages as the basis of democracy is called
qa.a: gram swaraj
qa.e: Gram swaraj means village self-rule.

qa.q: Which was a major weakness of local bodies before 1992?
qa.a: They lacked funds and elections were often irregular
qa.e: Dependence on States and irregular elections weakened them.

qa.q: Which committee recommended constitutional recognition for local government in 1986?
qa.a: L.M. Singhvi Committee
qa.e: The Singhvi Committee pushed for constitutional recognition.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Local bodies were weak before the 73rd Amendment. Reason (R): Local government was a State subject, and many States held irregular elections and gave few funds.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; State control and irregular elections explain the weakness.

qa.q: The Community Development Programme was launched in
qa.e: It was launched in 1952; the Balwantrai Mehta Committee followed in 1957.

qa.q: The 73rd Amendment relates to
qa.a: rural local bodies (panchayats)
qa.e: 73rd is for panchayats; 74th is for municipalities.

qa.q: What is the Gram Sabha?
qa.a: A body of all adult voters registered in a village
qa.e: Every adult voter of the village is a member of the Gram Sabha.

qa.q: Which is the district-level tier of panchayati raj?
qa.a: Zila Parishad
qa.e: The Zila Parishad is at the district level.

qa.q: What is the term of a panchayat body under the 73rd Amendment?
qa.a: 5 years
qa.e: All tiers have a five-year term.

qa.q: Which body conducts panchayat elections?
qa.a: The State Election Commission
qa.e: Each State has an independent State Election Commission for local elections.

qa.q: The intermediate tier (Panchayat Samiti) is found at the
qa.a: block level
qa.e: Panchayat Samitis function at the block level.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The 73rd Amendment ensured regular panchayat elections. Reason (R): It requires elections every five years and within six months of any early dissolution.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; mandatory timelines are why elections became regular.

qa.q: Both the 73rd and 74th Amendments came into force in
qa.e: Passed in 1992, they came into force in 1993.

qa.q: How many subjects are listed in the Eleventh Schedule?
qa.e: The Eleventh Schedule lists 29 subjects for panchayats.

qa.q: What fraction of seats in panchayats must at least be reserved for women?
qa.a: One-third
qa.e: The 73rd Amendment reserves not less than one-third.

qa.q: A Zila Parishad has 36 seats. What is the minimum number reserved for women?
qa.e: One-third of 36 is 12.

qa.q: How are seats reserved for SC and ST in panchayats?
qa.a: In proportion to their population in the area
qa.e: Reservation is proportional to SC/ST population.

qa.q: What does the State Finance Commission do?
qa.a: Reviews the finances of local bodies and recommends sharing of State revenue with them
qa.e: It is appointed every five years for local body finances.

qa.q: The PESA Act of 1996 deals with
qa.a: extending panchayat provisions to Scheduled Areas while respecting tribal customs
qa.e: PESA brings panchayati raj to Scheduled Areas.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Many subjects in the Eleventh Schedule have not been fully transferred to panchayats. Reason (R): These subjects are State subjects, and transfer depends on each State's laws.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; dependence on State laws explains incomplete transfer.

qa.q: Which subject is listed in the Eleventh Schedule?
qa.a: Drinking water
qa.e: Drinking water is among the 29 subjects; the others are Union subjects.

qa.q: The 74th Amendment deals with
qa.a: urban local bodies
qa.e: The 74th Amendment covers municipalities.

qa.q: How many subjects are listed in the Twelfth Schedule?
qa.e: The Twelfth Schedule lists 18 subjects for municipalities.

qa.q: A Nagar Panchayat is meant for
qa.a: an area in transition from rural to urban
qa.e: Nagar Panchayats serve transitional areas.

qa.q: Which urban local body is formed for larger cities?
qa.a: Municipal Corporation
qa.e: Large cities have Municipal Corporations.

qa.q: Which subject is in the Twelfth Schedule?
qa.a: Fire services
qa.e: Fire services are an urban local subject; minor irrigation is in the Eleventh Schedule.

qa.q: Which feature is common to both the 73rd and 74th Amendments?
qa.a: One-third reservation of seats for women
qa.e: Both reserve one-third seats for women; the tiers and subject lists differ.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Ward committees are set up in larger municipalities. Reason (R): Ward committees were created by the 73rd Amendment.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false: ward committees are part of the 74th Amendment on urban local bodies; the 73rd deals with panchayats.

qa.q: Which body conducts elections to municipalities?
qa.a: The State Election Commission
qa.e: Like panchayats, municipal elections are conducted by State Election Commissions.

qa.q: Which is a major achievement of the 73rd and 74th Amendments?
qa.a: Regular elections and a large number of elected local representatives, including women
qa.e: Regular elections and wide representation are the main achievements.

qa.q: Which is a major problem in the working of local bodies?
qa.a: Dependence on grants from State and central governments
qa.e: Limited own funds make them dependent.

qa.q: Why is devolution to local bodies often called 'limited'?
qa.a: State governments have transferred few subjects, funds and staff
qa.e: Real power depends on State-level transfer of functions, funds and functionaries.

qa.q: How has women's reservation in local bodies affected women's participation?
qa.a: It has brought lakhs of women into local leadership positions
qa.e: Reservation has greatly increased women's participation.

qa.q: Local bodies often implement schemes designed by higher governments. This means
qa.a: they have limited freedom to plan their own priorities
qa.e: Dependence reduces genuine self-government.

qa.q: What would most strengthen local self-government?
qa.a: Greater transfer of funds, functions and staff to local bodies
qa.e: Fiscal and administrative autonomy are needed.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Many local bodies cannot carry out their responsibilities fully. Reason (R): They have limited funds and depend on State and central grants.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; financial dependence explains why they cannot carry out duties fully.

qa.q: Which statement best evaluates the 73rd and 74th Amendments?
qa.a: They created a strong democratic base, but genuine self-government needs more financial and administrative autonomy
qa.e: A balanced view recognises both achievements and limits.

qa.q: Why is the Indian Constitution called a 'living document'?
qa.a: It adapts to changing circumstances while preserving its core values
qa.e: It grows through amendments and interpretation without losing its identity.

qa.q: How many times has the Indian Constitution been replaced since 1950?
qa.a: It has never been replaced, only amended
qa.e: India has had one constitution, amended over 100 times.

qa.q: Which country had four constitutions in the twentieth century (1918, 1924, 1936, 1977)?
qa.a: The Soviet Union
qa.e: The USSR adopted four constitutions.

qa.q: A constitution that can never be amended would most likely
qa.a: fail to adapt to new challenges and lose relevance
qa.e: Without flexibility a constitution cannot respond to change.

qa.q: India's Constitution has lasted because
qa.a: it balances stability with flexibility and has been respected by institutions
qa.e: Balance and institutional respect keep it alive.

qa.q: A constitution that is too easily changed by ordinary majorities would
qa.a: fail to protect core values and rights
qa.e: Core values need protection from passing majorities.

qa.q: Assertion (A): India's Constitution has continued for over seven decades. Reason (R): The 61st Amendment lowered the voting age to 18.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true, but the voting-age change does not explain the Constitution's survival; its balance of stability and flexibility does.

qa.q: France's present constitution dates from
qa.e: The Fifth Republic constitution dates from 1958.

qa.q: Which Article of the Constitution deals with the amendment procedure?
qa.a: Article 368
qa.e: Article 368 lays down the procedure.

qa.q: What does a 'special majority' for amendments mean?
qa.a: A majority of the total membership of the House and two-thirds of members present and voting
qa.e: Both conditions must be met in each House.

qa.q: Which provisions need ratification by half the States in addition to a special majority?
qa.a: Provisions affecting the federal structure, such as Centre–State distribution of powers
qa.e: Federal provisions require State ratification.

qa.q: A Lok Sabha of 543 members has 390 present and voting. What is the minimum number of 'yes' votes for a special majority?
qa.e: Two-thirds of 390 = 260, but a majority of total membership needs 272. So 272 is needed.

qa.q: Which of the following is changed by a simple majority and is NOT treated as an amendment under Article 368?
qa.a: Creating a new State by a law under Articles 2–4
qa.e: Articles 2–4 changes are made by ordinary law.

qa.q: Can a joint sitting be used to pass a constitutional amendment bill?
qa.a: No, each House must pass it separately
qa.e: Amendment bills must be passed by each House separately.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The Indian amendment procedure is a mix of rigidity and flexibility. Reason (R): Some provisions can be changed by simple majority, others need a special majority, and some also need State ratification.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the graded procedure is what creates the mix.

qa.q: Which is NOT part of India's amendment procedure?
qa.a: A national referendum
qa.e: India does not use referendums for amendments.

qa.q: The 15th Amendment (1963) raised the retirement age of High Court judges from 60 to
qa.e: It raised the age to 62.

qa.q: Which type of amendment was the 52nd Amendment (anti-defection law)?
qa.a: One passed through political consensus
qa.e: It had support across parties.

qa.q: Why were some amendments passed due to 'differing interpretations'?
qa.a: The judiciary and the government disagreed on what the Constitution meant
qa.e: Disagreements on property rights and amendment power led to amendments.

qa.q: Lowering the voting age to 18, a change backed across parties, was done by which amendment?
qa.a: 61st Amendment
qa.e: The 61st Amendment (1988).

qa.q: A large number of amendments in India mostly reflects
qa.a: adaptation through technical changes and political consensus
qa.e: Most amendments are practical or agreed changes.

qa.q: Which is an example of a technical amendment?
qa.a: Revising the salaries of judges (54th Amendment)
qa.e: Salary revision is administrative.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Many amendments to the Indian Constitution were passed with support from both ruling and opposition parties. Reason (R): Issues like anti-defection, voting age and local government enjoyed wide agreement.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; wide agreement on such issues explains consensus amendments.

qa.q: The 73rd and 74th Amendments are good examples of amendments based on
qa.a: political consensus
qa.e: They were supported widely across parties.

qa.q: Which words were added to the Preamble by the 42nd Amendment?
qa.a: Socialist, secular and integrity
qa.e: These three words came in 1976.

qa.q: The 42nd Amendment extended the term of the Lok Sabha from
qa.a: 5 to 6 years
qa.e: The 44th Amendment later restored the five-year term.

qa.q: Which amendment reversed many changes of the 42nd Amendment?
qa.a: 44th Amendment (1978)
qa.e: The 44th Amendment undid key changes after the Emergency.

qa.q: During which period were the 38th, 39th and 42nd Amendments passed?
qa.a: The internal Emergency of 1975–77
qa.e: They were passed during the Emergency.

qa.q: Why is the 42nd Amendment sometimes called a 'mini-Constitution'?
qa.a: It made very wide-ranging changes to many parts of the Constitution
qa.e: It changed the Preamble, rights, duties, Parliament's term and judicial review.

qa.q: The 39th Amendment sought to
qa.a: place the election of the Prime Minister beyond the scrutiny of courts
qa.e: It tried to protect the PM's election from judicial review.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The Emergency-era amendments are considered controversial. Reason (R): They were passed when opposition leaders were in jail and sought to curb the judiciary.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the circumstances and aims explain why they are controversial.

qa.q: Which change was made by the 44th Amendment?
qa.a: The right to property was removed from the list of Fundamental Rights
qa.e: These others were 42nd Amendment changes.

qa.q: Which case established the basic structure doctrine?
qa.a: Kesavananda Bharati (1973)
qa.e: Kesavananda Bharati is the landmark case.

qa.q: According to Kesavananda Bharati, Parliament
qa.a: can amend the Constitution but cannot alter its basic structure
qa.e: Amending power is wide but limited by the basic structure.

qa.q: Which of the following has been recognised as part of the basic structure?
qa.a: Judicial review
qa.e: Judicial review is a basic feature; the others are ordinary provisions.

qa.q: What did the Golaknath case (1967) decide?
qa.a: Parliament cannot amend Fundamental Rights
qa.e: Golaknath limited Parliament's power over Fundamental Rights.

qa.q: Why is the basic structure doctrine called a 'judicial contribution'?
qa.a: It was developed by the Supreme Court, not written in the Constitution's text
qa.e: The doctrine emerged from judicial interpretation.

qa.q: By what margin did the 13-judge bench decide Kesavananda Bharati?
qa.a: 7 to 6
qa.e: It was a narrow 7–6 majority.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The basic structure doctrine protects the core of the Constitution. Reason (R): It prevents Parliament from using its amending power to destroy essential features like democracy and secularism.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; limiting the amending power is how it protects the core.

qa.q: Which statement about the basic structure is correct?
qa.a: Courts identify its elements case by case; there is no exhaustive list
qa.e: It has evolved through judgments.

qa.q: In which case did the Supreme Court lay down a general 50% ceiling on reservations?
qa.a: Indra Sawhney (1992)
qa.e: Indra Sawhney set the 50% limit.

qa.q: How has the judiciary contributed to the Constitution as a living document?
qa.a: By interpreting provisions like Article 21 to include new rights
qa.e: Interpretation expands meaning without changing text.

qa.q: Which of these is an example of 'political maturity'?
qa.a: Governments accepting court verdicts even when they disagree
qa.e: Respecting institutions is a sign of maturity.

qa.q: The Constitution evolves through
qa.a: formal amendments, judicial interpretation and political practice
qa.e: All three routes shape the Constitution.

qa.q: Recognising the right to livelihood under Article 21 is an example of
qa.a: judicial interpretation
qa.e: The text did not change; the meaning grew.

qa.q: A change that alters the meaning but not the words of the Constitution comes through
qa.a: judicial interpretation
qa.e: Courts change meaning; amendments change text.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The Constitution of India is described as a living document. Reason (R): It has grown through amendments, judicial interpretation and political practice.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; these modes of growth are why it is called living.

qa.q: Which is a formal amendment rather than an interpretation?
qa.a: Lowering the voting age to 18
qa.e: The 61st Amendment changed the text; the others are judicial.

qa.q: What is meant by the 'philosophy of the Constitution'?
qa.a: The moral and political values underlying its provisions
qa.e: Philosophy refers to the values behind the text.

qa.q: Why is the Constitution called a means of democratic transformation?
qa.a: It enables peaceful social change, like breaking caste hierarchy, through constitutional means
qa.e: It channels change through democratic, peaceful means.

qa.q: Why should we go back to the Constituent Assembly Debates?
qa.a: They reveal the reasons and intentions behind provisions
qa.e: The debates show why provisions were adopted.

qa.q: The Constitution both limits state power and
qa.a: enables the state to bring about social justice
qa.e: It restrains and empowers the state.

qa.q: Which of these is an example of using constitutional means to break caste hierarchy?
qa.a: Abolition of untouchability under Article 17
qa.e: Article 17 directly targets caste-based discrimination.

qa.q: What do the Constituent Assembly Debates reveal besides the final decisions?
qa.a: The alternatives considered and the compromises made
qa.e: They show the reasoning process.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Studying the Constituent Assembly Debates helps in interpreting the Constitution. Reason (R): The debates show the reasons and values behind the provisions.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; knowing the reasons helps apply provisions to new questions.

qa.q: Concepts like rights, citizenship and democracy are studied in the philosophy of the Constitution to
qa.a: understand their meanings and how they are interpreted
qa.e: Philosophy clarifies meanings and interpretations.

qa.q: Which constitutional provision best reflects the commitment to individual freedom?
qa.a: Protection against arbitrary arrest
qa.e: It protects individual liberty from state power.

qa.q: Reservation of seats for SC and ST in legislatures reflects the value of
qa.a: social justice
qa.e: It addresses historical disadvantage.

qa.q: Why did the makers go beyond equal rights on paper?
qa.a: Because groups facing centuries of discrimination needed special measures to achieve real equality
qa.e: Special measures make equality real.

qa.q: The Constitution's approach to minorities can be described as
qa.a: community-sensitive: protecting the rights of religious and linguistic communities
qa.e: It protects communities as well as individuals.

qa.q: Which Articles protect the cultural and educational rights of minorities?
qa.a: Articles 29 and 30
qa.e: Articles 29–30 deal with minority rights.

qa.q: 'Compensatory discrimination' refers to
qa.a: special provisions that favour disadvantaged groups to make up for past injustice
qa.e: It is another term for affirmative action.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The Indian Constitution protects both individual and community rights. Reason (R): It recognises that Indian society consists of many communities with distinct identities.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; recognising India's communities is why community rights are protected.

qa.q: The commitment to individual freedom in the Constitution grew mainly out of
qa.a: the national movement's struggle against colonial repression
qa.e: Freedom was a central demand of the national movement.

qa.q: What is meant by 'principled distance' in Indian secularism?
qa.a: The state keeps a distance from religion but may intervene to promote equality and freedom
qa.e: Principled distance allows reformist intervention.

qa.q: Which is an example of the state intervening in religion for reform?
qa.a: Laws opening temples to people of all castes
qa.e: Temple-entry laws promote equality.

qa.q: Adopting universal adult franchise from the start showed
qa.a: faith in ordinary people's ability to choose their government
qa.e: It trusted all adults equally.

qa.q: How does the Indian Constitution view national identity?
qa.a: Indian identity coexists with other identities like religion, region and language
qa.e: It is a plural, accommodating identity.

qa.q: Special provisions for States like Nagaland and Mizoram reflect
qa.a: asymmetric federalism
qa.e: Asymmetry recognises regional diversity.

qa.q: Religious freedom under the Indian Constitution belongs to
qa.a: both individuals and religious communities
qa.e: Individuals and communities both have religious freedom.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Indian secularism is different from the Western idea of strict separation. Reason (R): The Indian state can engage with religion to promote equality, e.g. against untouchability.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; reform-oriented engagement is the key difference.

qa.q: Which statement about India's Constitution and religion is correct?
qa.a: There is no official religion of the state
qa.e: India is a secular state.

qa.q: Which of these is a procedural achievement of the Constituent Assembly?
qa.a: Decision-making by consensus
qa.e: Consensus is a procedural, not substantive, achievement.

qa.q: 'Faith in political deliberation' means
qa.a: belief in open, reasoned discussion before reaching decisions
qa.e: Deliberation means reasoned debate.

qa.q: Why did the Assembly try to reach consensus rather than rely only on majority votes?
qa.a: To make the Constitution acceptable to all groups, including minorities
qa.e: Consensus builds legitimacy.

qa.q: A spirit of accommodation means
qa.a: willingness to adjust one's position to include others' concerns
qa.e: Accommodation is about making room for others.

qa.q: How did the procedures of the Assembly add to the Constitution's authority?
qa.a: Groups felt their views were heard, so they accepted the outcome
qa.e: Fair procedures produce legitimacy.

qa.q: The compromise on official language is an example of
qa.a: accommodation and compromise
qa.e: Different language groups were accommodated.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The Constituent Assembly is admired for how it worked, not just for what it produced. Reason (R): It practised deliberation, accommodation and consensus while making decisions.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; these practices are why its procedure is admired.

qa.q: Deferring some contentious decisions helped the Assembly to
qa.a: avoid deep divisions and keep broad agreement
qa.e: Deferral can preserve agreement on core issues.

qa.q: Which is a common criticism of the Indian Constitution?
qa.a: It is unwieldy and very long
qa.e: Length and detail are frequently criticised.

qa.q: The criticism that the Constitution is 'unrepresentative' is based on the fact that
qa.a: the Constituent Assembly was not elected by universal adult franchise
qa.e: Members were indirectly elected.

qa.q: What is a valid response to the criticism that the Constitution is 'alien'?
qa.a: Borrowed ideas were adapted to Indian conditions and blended with Indian concerns
qa.e: Adaptation, not copying, answers this criticism.

qa.q: Which is identified as a limitation of the Constitution?
qa.a: Issues of gender justice within the family were left largely unresolved
qa.e: Family-related gender justice is a noted limitation.

qa.q: Putting the right to work in the Directive Principles rather than Fundamental Rights is seen as a limitation because
qa.a: these socio-economic rights cannot be enforced in court
qa.e: Non-justiciability weakens such rights.

qa.q: A 'centralised idea of national unity' as a limitation means that
qa.a: the Constitution gives the Centre strong powers, which some see as weakening regional autonomy
qa.e: Strong Centre is a noted limitation.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The criticism that the Assembly was unrepresentative is only partly valid. Reason (R): Though indirectly elected, the Assembly had members from diverse groups and its debates reflected many views.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the diversity of members and views is why the criticism is only partly valid.

qa.q: Which response best answers the criticism that the Constitution is unwieldy?
qa.a: Its detail reflects India's size, diversity and the need to settle many issues clearly
qa.e: Detail was needed for a large, diverse country.

qa.q: How does political theory understand politics?
qa.a: As the process of collective decision-making and pursuit of a good society
qa.e: It sees politics as a broad social process.

qa.q: Which is an example of politics in the broad sense?
qa.a: Villagers negotiating with the panchayat over water distribution
qa.e: Collective decision-making is politics.

qa.q: Why do many people view politics negatively?
qa.a: They associate it with self-interest, manipulation and corruption
qa.e: This is the common negative image.

qa.q: Which of the following is NOT part of politics in the broad sense?
qa.a: Choosing a personal hobby on your own
qa.e: Purely private choices that do not involve collective decisions are not politics.

qa.q: A people's movement demanding cleaner rivers is an example of
qa.a: politics as citizens' participation
qa.e: Movements are part of politics.

qa.q: The broad view of politics emphasises that
qa.a: politics is an important part of any society and citizens shape it
qa.e: Citizens are participants in politics.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Politics is necessary in every society. Reason (R): Societies need ways to make collective decisions and resolve disagreements.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the need for collective decisions is why politics is necessary.

qa.q: Which statement best describes the relationship between politics and a 'good society'?
qa.a: Politics is the means by which people debate and pursue a good society
qa.e: Politics involves debating what is good and just.

qa.q: Which of these is a central concern of political theory?
qa.a: Clarifying the meaning of concepts like freedom, equality and justice
qa.e: Political theory examines ideas and principles.

qa.q: Which thinker argued that freedom is a fundamental right of humanity?
qa.a: Rousseau
qa.e: Rousseau is associated with freedom as fundamental.

qa.q: Who argued that equality is as crucial as freedom?
qa.a: Karl Marx
qa.e: Marx stressed equality.

qa.q: In which book did Gandhi discuss the meaning of swaraj?
qa.a: Hind Swaraj
qa.e: Gandhi wrote Hind Swaraj in 1909.

qa.q: Ambedkar argued that the Scheduled Castes
qa.a: should be considered a minority and given special protection
qa.e: He argued for special protection.

qa.q: Political theory examines how concepts are
qa.a: applied in practice and whether they are applied fairly
qa.e: It studies both meaning and application.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Political theory draws on thinkers across centuries. Reason (R): Ideas about freedom, equality and justice have been debated since ancient times.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; long-running debate is why it draws on many thinkers.

qa.q: Plato and Aristotle belonged to
qa.a: ancient Greece
qa.e: Both were ancient Greek philosophers.

qa.q: What does political theory do when it is put into practice?
qa.a: Applies concepts like equality to real issues and tests beliefs through argument
qa.e: It connects concepts with real debates.

qa.q: Debating whether reservations are fair mainly involves which concept?
qa.a: Equality
qa.e: Reservations raise questions about equality.

qa.q: Why is reasoned argument important in political theory?
qa.a: It helps examine whether beliefs are justified and consistent
qa.e: Reasoned argument tests beliefs.

qa.q: Applying the concept of equality shows that
qa.a: it may mean identical treatment or special help for the disadvantaged
qa.e: Concepts can have multiple meanings.

qa.q: Which activity best puts political theory into practice?
qa.a: Debating whether a school dress code is fair, with reasons on both sides
qa.e: Debate applies concepts to real situations.

qa.q: What is the goal of debate in political theory?
qa.a: To arrive at better-reasoned, more defensible positions
qa.e: Debate improves reasoning.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Political theory is useful in public debates. Reason (R): It clarifies concepts and helps weigh reasons on different sides.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; clarifying concepts and weighing reasons is how it helps.

qa.q: A student says, 'Free coaching for some students is unfair because everyone must be treated identically.' Which idea challenges this?
qa.a: Equality can also mean giving extra help to those who are disadvantaged
qa.e: Equality of opportunity may need differential treatment.

qa.q: Who benefits from studying political theory?
qa.a: Politicians, officials, lawyers, activists and ordinary citizens
qa.e: It is useful for everyone in a democracy.

qa.q: How does political theory help ordinary citizens?
qa.a: It helps them form informed and reasoned opinions on public issues
qa.e: It sharpens reasoning, not dictating choices.

qa.q: Studying political theory encourages tolerance because
qa.a: understanding other viewpoints helps us examine our own prejudices
qa.e: Understanding others reduces prejudice.

qa.q: A debate on banning a book mainly involves which concept?
qa.a: Freedom
qa.e: Censorship raises questions of freedom of expression.

qa.q: A dispute about whether workers get fair wages for their work mainly involves
qa.a: equality and justice
qa.e: Fair wages raise questions of equality and justice.

qa.q: Why is a reasoning citizenry important for democracy?
qa.a: Citizens who reason well can judge policies and hold leaders accountable
qa.e: Informed citizens strengthen democracy.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Political theory is relevant to students who will not become politicians. Reason (R): As citizens, they will vote and take positions on public issues that need reasoned judgment.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; citizenship itself requires reasoned judgment.

qa.q: Which skill does political theory most directly develop?
qa.a: Identifying which concept is at stake in a situation and reasoning about it
qa.e: It develops conceptual and reasoning skills.

qa.q: Which book is Nelson Mandela's autobiography?
qa.a: Long Walk to Freedom
qa.e: Mandela's autobiography is Long Walk to Freedom.

qa.q: 'Freedom from Fear' is associated with
qa.a: Aung San Suu Kyi
qa.e: Suu Kyi of Myanmar wrote it.

qa.q: Mandela struggled against which system?
qa.a: Apartheid in South Africa
qa.e: Apartheid was a system of racial segregation.

qa.q: How many years did Nelson Mandela spend in prison?
qa.e: He was imprisoned for 27 years.

qa.q: According to Suu Kyi, why is fear important in thinking about freedom?
qa.a: Fear of others' reactions can prevent us from acting freely, so overcoming it is part of freedom
qa.e: Freedom requires courage to overcome fear.

qa.q: What do the struggles of Mandela and Suu Kyi show about freedom?
qa.a: Freedom involves challenging unjust constraints imposed by governments or society
qa.e: Their struggles were against unjust constraints.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Nelson Mandela's struggle is described as a struggle for freedom. Reason (R): Apartheid denied freedom and equality to non-white South Africans.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; apartheid's denial of freedom is exactly why his struggle was a struggle for freedom.

qa.q: Why is freedom valued?
qa.a: It allows individuals to make their own choices and develop their capacities
qa.e: Choice and self-development are core.

qa.q: Freedom understood as 'absence of external constraints' means
qa.a: being able to make choices without others controlling or preventing us
qa.e: This is the basic negative view of freedom.

qa.q: The fuller view of freedom adds the idea of
qa.a: expanding the conditions in which people can develop their talents
qa.e: Freedom also requires enabling conditions.

qa.q: Gandhi's idea of swaraj included
qa.a: rule over oneself as well as freedom from foreign rule
qa.e: Swaraj meant self-rule at individual and social levels.

qa.q: Which of the following is a social constraint on freedom?
qa.a: Caste-based exclusion from public places
qa.e: Social inequality constrains freedom.

qa.q: Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose's idea of freedom was
qa.a: all-round freedom for individuals and society, rich and poor, men and women
qa.e: He emphasised freedom for all.

qa.q: A poor child cannot attend school because she must work to support her family. Her freedom is constrained mainly by
qa.a: economic inequality
qa.e: Poverty is the constraint here.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Freedom requires more than the absence of legal bans. Reason (R): Social and economic conditions can prevent people from exercising choices that the law allows.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; such conditions are why freedom needs more than removing bans.

qa.q: In which year did Gandhi write Hind Swaraj?
qa.e: Hind Swaraj was written in 1909.

qa.q: Why are some constraints necessary in society?
qa.a: To prevent harm and allow people with different views to live together peacefully
qa.e: Constraints protect freedom for all.

qa.q: Which constraint is most clearly justified?
qa.a: A law punishing violence against others
qa.e: Preventing violence protects others.

qa.q: Liberalism as a political ideology emphasises
qa.a: individual liberty and toleration
qa.e: Liberals value the individual and tolerance.

qa.q: What makes a constraint unjustified?
qa.a: When it is imposed to dominate or discriminate without preventing harm
qa.e: Domination and discrimination make constraints unjust.

qa.q: A traffic rule restricts how fast you can drive. Political theory would see this as
qa.a: a justified constraint that protects others
qa.e: It prevents harm to others.

qa.q: Which statement about liberalism is correct?
qa.a: It values toleration of differing views and opinions
qa.e: Toleration is central to liberalism.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Some constraints on freedom are acceptable. Reason (R): Constraints that prevent harm to others help everyone enjoy freedom.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; protecting others' freedom is why some constraints are acceptable.

qa.q: The central question in debates about constraints is
qa.a: which constraints are justified and which are not
qa.e: The issue is justification, not existence.

qa.q: According to Mill's harm principle, when can society rightfully restrict a person's liberty?
qa.a: Only to prevent harm to others
qa.e: Harm to others is the only justification.

qa.q: In which work did J.S. Mill set out the harm principle?
qa.a: On Liberty
qa.e: On Liberty (1859).

qa.q: A 'self-regarding' action is one that
qa.a: mainly affects the person who performs it
qa.e: Mill says such actions should be left free.

qa.q: For a minor harm, Mill recommends
qa.a: social disapproval, not the force of law
qa.e: Mill distinguishes minor and serious harm.

qa.q: Which action would Mill most clearly allow the law to restrict?
qa.a: Drunk driving that endangers others
qa.e: Serious risk of harm to others justifies legal restriction.

qa.q: Why is the harm principle said to protect a wide area of freedom?
qa.a: Because it sets a high bar — only harm to others justifies interference
qa.e: Restrictions need a strong reason.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Mill would oppose banning a book merely because many people find it offensive. Reason (R): Under the harm principle, offence alone is not the same as harm to others.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; since offence is not harm, the principle would not justify a ban.

qa.q: Playing very loud music late at night in a residential area is, for Mill, an example of
qa.a: an other-regarding action causing minor harm, deserving social disapproval
qa.e: It affects others but the harm is minor.

qa.q: Negative liberty refers to
qa.a: an area of non-interference where a person is free from external constraints
qa.e: Negative liberty is 'freedom from'.

qa.q: Positive liberty emphasises
qa.a: the conditions needed for individuals to develop their capacities
qa.e: Positive liberty is 'freedom to'.

qa.q: Who distinguished between 'two concepts of liberty'?
qa.a: Isaiah Berlin
qa.e: Berlin's 1958 essay drew this distinction.

qa.q: Free public education to help children develop their abilities is an example of
qa.a: positive liberty
qa.e: It creates enabling conditions.

qa.q: Freedom of expression is usually considered part of
qa.a: the minimum area of non-interference (negative liberty)
qa.e: Expression is central to the private sphere.

qa.q: Which question is associated with positive liberty?
qa.a: Who governs me, and do I have the conditions to develop myself?
qa.e: Positive liberty concerns self-mastery and conditions.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Positive liberty is concerned only with non-interference by the state. Reason (R): Positive liberty stresses enabling conditions such as education and health for self-development.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: non-interference is the core of negative liberty. R correctly describes positive liberty.

qa.q: A law protecting a person from arrest without reason protects
qa.a: negative liberty
qa.e: It shields a person from interference.

qa.q: Which of the following is often cited in debates on censorship in India?
qa.a: The ban on importing The Satanic Verses
qa.e: It is a classic example in freedom of expression debates.

qa.q: What do supporters of free expression argue about banning books?
qa.a: Bans are short-term solutions; disagreement should be met with argument
qa.e: They prefer debate to suppression.

qa.q: Under the Indian Constitution, restrictions on freedom of speech must be
qa.a: reasonable
qa.e: Article 19 allows only reasonable restrictions.

qa.q: Which constraint needs stronger justification?
qa.a: One imposed without the consent of those affected
qa.e: Imposed constraints require stronger reasons.

qa.q: The disruption of the shooting of Deepa Mehta's film Water raised questions about
qa.a: freedom of artistic expression
qa.e: It is an example in debates on expression.

qa.q: Which reason is accepted in the Constitution for restricting speech?
qa.a: Public order
qa.e: Public order is a listed ground for reasonable restriction.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Freedom of expression is considered part of the minimum area of non-interference. Reason (R): Without it, people cannot freely form, share and test their ideas.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the role of expression in developing ideas explains its special protection.

qa.q: A student council debates and votes on a dress code. This is an example of
qa.a: a constraint accepted voluntarily through participation
qa.e: Participation makes the constraint voluntary.

qa.q: What does 'equality of opportunity' mean?
qa.a: Everyone should have equal chances to develop their talents and pursue their goals
qa.e: It focuses on equal chances, not identical results.

qa.q: Which is an example of a social inequality?
qa.a: Women being paid less than men for the same work
qa.e: Unequal pay is created by social arrangements.

qa.q: Natural inequalities arise from
qa.a: differences in people's abilities and talents
qa.e: Natural inequalities come from inborn differences.

qa.q: Why should social inequalities be corrected?
qa.a: They are created by society, are unjust, and can be changed
qa.e: Being man-made and unjust, they should be removed.

qa.q: Which idea lies at the core of the ideal of equality?
qa.a: All human beings have equal worth and deserve equal respect
qa.e: Equal moral worth is the basis of equality.

qa.q: Some differences once considered 'natural', such as claims about women's inferior abilities, are now seen as
qa.a: social inequalities produced by prejudice and lack of opportunity
qa.e: Many supposed natural differences were socially created.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Equality of opportunity does not mean identical outcomes. Reason (R): People with equal chances may still differ in results because of their efforts and abilities.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; differences in effort and ability under equal chances explain different outcomes.

qa.q: A brilliant student cannot attend college because her family cannot afford fees. This shows a lack of
qa.a: equality of opportunity
qa.e: Economic barriers deny her equal chances.

qa.q: Political equality includes
qa.a: equal right to vote, contest elections and enjoy civil liberties
qa.e: Political equality concerns citizenship rights.

qa.q: Why is political equality alone not enough?
qa.a: Social and economic inequalities can still limit people's real opportunities
qa.e: Equal votes do not guarantee equal life chances.

qa.q: Social equality is mainly concerned with
qa.a: equal life chances, such as access to education and health, and ending discrimination
qa.e: Social equality focuses on life chances and dignity.

qa.q: Economic equality mainly aims to
qa.a: reduce large gaps in income and wealth
qa.e: The concern is extreme gaps.

qa.q: A minimum wage law is a measure of
qa.a: economic equality
qa.e: It reduces income gaps.

qa.q: Which dimension does ending caste discrimination in temples and wells address most directly?
qa.a: Social equality
qa.e: It addresses discrimination and dignity.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Economic inequality can weaken political equality. Reason (R): The very rich can use their wealth to gain greater influence over politics.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; unequal influence through wealth is how economic inequality weakens political equality.

qa.q: Universal adult franchise reflects which dimension of equality?
qa.a: Political equality
qa.e: Equal votes for all adults.

qa.q: What is patriarchy?
qa.a: A social system that values men more than women and gives men power over women
qa.e: Feminists identify patriarchy as the source of gender inequality.

qa.q: Feminists argue that inequality between men and women is
qa.a: created by society, not by nature
qa.e: Patriarchy is socially constructed.

qa.q: The distinction between sex and gender is that
qa.a: sex refers to biological differences, gender to socially created roles
qa.e: Feminists use this distinction to challenge social roles.

qa.q: Which is a central aim of socialism?
qa.a: Minimising inequalities and distributing resources justly
qa.e: Socialists seek to reduce inequality.

qa.q: Which Indian socialist identified five inequalities to be fought simultaneously?
qa.a: Ram Manohar Lohia
qa.e: Lohia gave the idea of sapta kranti.

qa.q: Which of the following was NOT one of Lohia's five inequalities?
qa.a: Inequality between States in Rajya Sabha seats
qa.e: His five were man–woman, skin colour, caste, colonial rule, and economic.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Feminists argue that gender roles can be changed. Reason (R): They see gender roles as socially constructed rather than determined by biology.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; social construction is why they can be changed.

qa.q: Lohia's 'sapta kranti' means
qa.a: seven revolutions
qa.e: Five inequalities plus two revolutions — for civil liberties and non-violence.

qa.q: What is formal equality?
qa.a: Removing legal privileges and discrimination so everyone is equal before the law
qa.e: Formal equality is equality in law.

qa.q: Why may equality require differential treatment?
qa.a: Because people starting from unequal positions need extra help to have real equal chances
qa.e: Equal treatment of unequals can perpetuate inequality.

qa.q: Which is an example of affirmative action?
qa.a: Reservation of seats in colleges for disadvantaged groups
qa.e: Reservations correct historic disadvantage.

qa.q: Building ramps in public buildings for wheelchair users is an example of
qa.a: equality through differential treatment
qa.e: Meeting special needs promotes equality.

qa.q: Abolishing a law that denied women the right to vote is an example of
qa.a: establishing formal equality
qa.e: It removes a legal barrier.

qa.q: Which statement about the debate on reservations is most balanced?
qa.a: Supporters see them as needed for social equality; critics question criteria and effects, so arguments must be weighed
qa.e: Political theory weighs reasons on both sides.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Affirmative action is consistent with the ideal of equality. Reason (R): It aims to correct accumulated disadvantages that prevent equal opportunity.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; correcting disadvantage is why it serves equality.

qa.q: A student says giving scholarships only to students from poor families is unfair. Which concept best answers her?
qa.a: Differential treatment to achieve equality of opportunity
qa.e: Extra help for the disadvantaged creates equal chances.

qa.q: In ancient Indian society, justice was associated with
qa.a: dharma
qa.e: Upholding dharma was a king's duty.

qa.q: Confucius argued that kings should maintain justice by
qa.a: punishing wrongdoers and rewarding the virtuous
qa.e: This is Confucius's view of justice.

qa.q: In which work does Socrates discuss justice with others?
qa.a: Plato's Republic
qa.e: Plato's Republic contains these dialogues.

qa.q: Kant's idea of human dignity means
qa.a: every person should be treated as an end in themselves, not merely as a means
qa.e: Kant's principle of respect for persons.

qa.q: According to Socrates in the Republic, justice
qa.a: involves the well-being of all, not the advantage of the stronger
qa.e: Socrates rejects 'might is right'.

qa.q: Which common idea links different traditions of justice?
qa.a: Giving each person their due
qa.e: Justice is about fair dues.

qa.q: Assertion (A): For Kant, justice requires respecting every person. Reason (R): Kant held that every human being possesses dignity.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; human dignity is why respect for every person is required.

qa.q: A boss treats an employee merely as a tool to earn profits, ignoring her well-being. Which thinker's idea most clearly condemns this?
qa.a: Immanuel Kant
qa.e: Kant says people must never be treated merely as means.

qa.q: The principle of 'equal treatment for equals' means
qa.a: people who share a common humanity should not be discriminated against on grounds like caste or gender
qa.e: It forbids unjust discrimination.

qa.q: Proportionate justice means
qa.a: rewards should be in proportion to effort, skill and risk
qa.e: It ties rewards to contribution.

qa.q: Giving extra exam time to a student with a disability reflects
qa.a: recognition of special needs
qa.e: Special needs justify extra help.

qa.q: Women and men teachers in a school receive the same pay for the same work. This applies
qa.a: equal treatment for equals
qa.e: Same work, same pay.

qa.q: A firm pays a deep-sea diver more than an office assistant. Which principle can justify this?
qa.a: Proportionate justice
qa.e: Higher risk and skill can justify higher pay.

qa.q: Why must a just society balance the three principles?
qa.a: Because they can conflict in particular situations
qa.e: Balancing is needed when principles pull apart.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Recognising special needs can be consistent with justice. Reason (R): People with disabilities or historic disadvantages may need extra help to be treated fairly.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; extra help for disadvantage is why it fits justice.

qa.q: A scholarship for students from communities that faced historic discrimination best reflects
qa.a: recognition of special needs
qa.e: It addresses disadvantage.

qa.q: Social justice mainly concerns
qa.a: fair distribution of goods, opportunities and services
qa.e: Distribution is central to social justice.

qa.q: Which is an example of a redistributive measure in India?
qa.a: Land reforms giving land to the landless
qa.e: Land reforms redistribute resources.

qa.q: Why were reservations introduced in education and jobs?
qa.a: To redistribute opportunities to groups facing historic disadvantage
qa.e: Reservations aim at fair access.

qa.q: What is the main debate in just distribution?
qa.a: Whether special treatment for disadvantaged groups or equal opportunity for individuals is fairer
qa.e: This is the central debate.

qa.q: Restricting land purchases by outsiders in tribal areas aims to
qa.a: protect local communities and their resources
qa.e: It protects vulnerable communities.

qa.q: A just distribution aims to ensure that
qa.a: everyone can live a dignified life with equal opportunities
qa.e: Dignity and opportunity for all.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Abolition of untouchability is a measure of social justice. Reason (R): It removes a deep social disadvantage imposed on certain groups.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; removing such disadvantage is why it serves social justice.

qa.q: Political theory's approach to debates on special treatment is to
qa.a: examine the arguments on both sides with reasons
qa.e: Reasoned examination is the method.

qa.q: Who proposed the 'veil of ignorance'?
qa.a: John Rawls
qa.e: Rawls in A Theory of Justice.

qa.q: Behind the veil of ignorance, people do NOT know
qa.a: their own future position, such as class, gender or talents
qa.e: They do not know their social position.

qa.q: According to Rawls, rational people behind the veil would choose rules that
qa.a: protect the worst-off members of society
qa.e: Not knowing their position, they would guard against the worst outcome.

qa.q: Rawls's argument relies mainly on
qa.a: rational thinking under uncertainty about one's position
qa.e: Rationality, not altruism, drives the choice.

qa.q: Why does the veil of ignorance help produce fair rules?
qa.a: It forces people to think impartially, without bias towards their own position
qa.e: Impartiality yields fairness.

qa.q: Rawls's book A Theory of Justice was published in
qa.e: It was published in 1971.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Rules chosen behind the veil of ignorance are likely to be fair. Reason (R): People choosing them cannot favour their own position because they do not know it.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; inability to favour oneself is why the rules are fair.

qa.q: Which policy is most consistent with Rawls's theory?
qa.a: Need-based support for the poorest members of society
qa.e: Rawls favours protecting the worst-off.

qa.q: Which of the following is a minimum basic need for a just society?
qa.a: Adequate nutrition and health care
qa.e: Basic needs include food, health, housing, education.

qa.q: Free-market supporters argue that
qa.a: open competition rewards talent and effort and gives choice
qa.e: They value competition and efficiency.

qa.q: Supporters of state intervention argue that
qa.a: markets tend to favour those who are already privileged
qa.e: Without resources, the poor cannot compete fairly.

qa.q: The Public Distribution System is an example of
qa.a: state action to meet basic needs
qa.e: It provides subsidised food grain.

qa.q: Why might a poor child be unable to compete fairly in a free market for education?
qa.a: The family lacks resources to pay for good schooling
qa.e: Lack of resources limits opportunity.

qa.q: A mixed approach to social justice means
qa.a: using markets for many goods while the state ensures basic needs and fair chances
qa.e: Most societies combine both.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Governments run programmes like employment guarantees and subsidised food. Reason (R): Markets alone may not ensure basic needs for the poorest.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the limits of markets are why such programmes exist.

qa.q: Which argument would a free-market supporter most likely make?
qa.a: The state should ensure a basic minimum but let competition decide most outcomes
qa.e: Limited state role with markets.

qa.q: What is a right?
qa.a: An entitlement or justified claim recognised by society and the state
qa.e: Rights are justified claims.

qa.q: Why are some claims recognised as rights?
qa.a: They are necessary for a life of dignity and well-being
qa.e: Dignity and well-being justify rights.

qa.q: Which of these is a desire rather than a right?
qa.a: Owning a luxury car
qa.e: Luxury is not necessary for dignity.

qa.q: A claim to be the only person allowed to use a public library is not a right because
qa.a: it denies the same claim to others and is not essential for anyone's dignity
qa.e: Rights must be available to all.

qa.q: Who must respect a person's rights?
qa.a: Other people and the state
qa.e: Rights create obligations for others and the state.

qa.q: Which claim best fits the idea of a right?
qa.a: Clean drinking water for every household
qa.e: Water is essential for life and dignity.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Not every want can be called a right. Reason (R): Rights are claims justified as essential for the dignity and well-being of all.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the justification test is why wants are not automatically rights.

qa.q: A right is best described as
qa.a: a justified claim
qa.e: Justification is the key.

qa.q: According to natural rights theory, rights come from
qa.a: nature or God
qa.e: Natural rights are not granted by rulers.

qa.q: Which three rights were identified as natural rights?
qa.a: Life, liberty and property
qa.e: These were the classic natural rights.

qa.q: Human rights are rights that people have because
qa.a: they are human beings
qa.e: Humanity alone is the basis.

qa.q: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights was adopted by the UN General Assembly in
qa.e: It was adopted on 10 December 1948.

qa.q: Why was natural rights theory used against absolute rulers?
qa.a: Because rights not granted by rulers could not be taken away by them
qa.e: It limited arbitrary power.

qa.q: Which is an example of an expanding claim to rights?
qa.a: The right to a clean environment
qa.e: New rights reflect new needs and threats.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Human rights are considered universal. Reason (R): Human rights apply only to citizens of democratic countries.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false: human rights belong to all persons simply because they are human, whatever their country.

qa.q: Natural rights theory was developed mainly by political theorists of the
qa.a: 17th and 18th centuries
qa.e: It was an early modern idea.

qa.q: How do rights become effective in practice?
qa.a: When they are recognised and protected by laws and constitutions
qa.e: Legal recognition makes rights enforceable.

qa.q: Rights limit the state and also
qa.a: require the state to take positive action
qa.e: The state must respect and promote rights.

qa.q: The right to vote is an example of a
qa.a: political right
qa.e: Political rights allow participation in governance.

qa.q: The right to a fair trial is classified as a
qa.a: civil liberty
qa.e: Civil liberties protect individuals against arbitrary state action.

qa.q: The right to a minimum wage is an example of an
qa.a: economic right
qa.e: Economic rights address basic needs.

qa.q: Education in one's mother tongue is an example of a
qa.a: cultural right
qa.e: Cultural rights protect language and culture.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Political rights help citizens participate in governance. Reason (R): They include the right to vote, contest elections and form political parties.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; these participatory rights are what make governance participatory.

qa.q: Which right best protects a person who wants to criticise government policy peacefully?
qa.a: Freedom of expression (a civil liberty)
qa.e: Expression is a civil liberty.

qa.q: Which is an obligation that rights place on the state?
qa.a: Protecting rights from violation by others
qa.e: The state must respect and protect rights.

qa.q: Which responsibility do rights place on citizens?
qa.a: Respecting the rights of others
qa.e: Rights are shared and must be respected mutually.

qa.q: Freedom of the press and the right to privacy can conflict when
qa.a: a newspaper publishes private information without consent
qa.e: Such cases require balancing two rights.

qa.q: Why are safeguards important when the state restricts liberties for security?
qa.a: Such powers can be misused against innocent people or critics
qa.e: Safeguards prevent abuse.

qa.q: Which is an example of the security versus civil liberties debate?
qa.a: Surveillance and preventive detention laws
qa.e: These involve trade-offs between security and liberty.

qa.q: Using rights with concern for future generations, e.g. protecting the environment, is an example of
qa.a: responsible use of rights for the common good
qa.e: Rights include responsibility to others.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Rights and responsibilities go together. Reason (R): The rights each person enjoys depend on others respecting them and on everyone using rights responsibly.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; mutual respect and responsible use explain why they go together.

qa.q: A government proposes unlimited phone tapping without any oversight. Which concern would a defender of civil liberties raise?
qa.a: It could be misused and violate privacy without safeguards
qa.e: Unchecked surveillance threatens liberty.

qa.q: Citizenship is best defined as
qa.a: full and equal membership of a political community
qa.e: This is the definition in political theory.

qa.q: Which is an obligation of citizens?
qa.a: Obeying laws and paying taxes
qa.e: Citizenship carries obligations.

qa.q: Treating migrants from other States as 'outsiders' raises a question about
qa.a: equal citizenship rights
qa.e: Migrants are equal citizens.

qa.q: The US civil rights movement struggled for
qa.a: equal citizenship rights for African Americans against segregation
qa.e: It fought racial segregation.

qa.q: Which leader is associated with the US civil rights movement?
qa.a: Martin Luther King Jr.
qa.e: MLK led the movement in the 1950s–60s.

qa.q: Full and equal membership in India includes the right to
qa.a: move, reside and work anywhere in the country
qa.e: These rights are protected by the Constitution.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Citizenship is a status that involves both rights and obligations. Reason (R): Citizens expect protection and rights from the state and in turn have duties towards the community.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the two-way relationship is why citizenship involves both.

qa.q: A city authority refuses to give ration cards to migrant workers from another State though they live there. This is a problem of
qa.a: denial of equal citizenship
qa.e: Equal citizens deserve equal access to services.

qa.q: Which three kinds of rights did T.H. Marshall link with citizenship?
qa.a: Civil, political and social rights
qa.e: Marshall's classic three categories.

qa.q: Social rights in Marshall's scheme include
qa.a: education, health and welfare
qa.e: Social rights relate to well-being.

qa.q: Why does equal citizenship sometimes require different policies for different groups?
qa.a: Groups have different needs and face different disadvantages
qa.e: Different needs require tailored responses.

qa.q: Slum dwellers often lack
qa.a: secure housing, sanitation and clean water
qa.e: They lack services despite being citizens.

qa.q: For tribal and forest communities, equal citizenship involves
qa.a: protecting their livelihood and way of life linked to land and forests
qa.e: Their resources and culture matter.

qa.q: The right to a fair trial belongs to which of Marshall's categories?
qa.a: Civil rights
qa.e: Fair trial is a civil right.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The urban poor are important to equal citizenship debates. Reason (R): They contribute to city life as workers and vendors but often lack basic services.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the gap between contribution and access is why they matter.

qa.q: Recognising street vendors' right to earn a livelihood in designated zones promotes
qa.a: equal citizenship for the urban poor
qa.e: It secures livelihood rights.

qa.q: Which law governs citizenship in India along with Part II of the Constitution?
qa.a: The Citizenship Act, 1955
qa.e: The Citizenship Act, 1955 is the main law.

qa.q: Which is NOT a way of acquiring Indian citizenship under the Citizenship Act, 1955?
qa.a: By buying property in India
qa.e: Property ownership does not confer citizenship.

qa.q: Who are stateless people?
qa.a: People who are not recognised as citizens by any state
qa.e: They lack the protection of citizenship.

qa.q: The Indian Constitution's conception of citizenship can be described as
qa.a: inclusive and democratic
qa.e: It is not based on religion, caste or language.

qa.q: Naturalisation means
qa.a: acquiring citizenship after living in a country for a required period and meeting conditions
qa.e: It is citizenship by application after residence.

qa.q: What is the ideal of universal citizenship?
qa.a: Full and equal membership should be available to all within a state
qa.e: It opposes exclusion within the state.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Refugees often face serious hardships. Reason (R): Without citizenship, they may lack the legal protection and rights a state provides.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; lack of citizenship protection explains their hardships.

qa.q: Common bases for citizenship used by nation-states include
qa.a: birth, descent and naturalisation
qa.e: These are the common legal bases.

qa.q: Global citizenship is based on the idea that
qa.a: all people share a common humanity beyond national borders
qa.e: Shared humanity is its basis.

qa.q: Which problem most clearly needs global cooperation?
qa.a: Climate change
qa.e: Climate change crosses borders.

qa.q: What is a main criticism of global citizenship?
qa.a: There is no world government to guarantee people's rights
qa.e: Rights still mostly depend on national states.

qa.q: How can national and global citizenship be combined?
qa.a: By being responsible citizens of one's country while caring about global problems
qa.e: Both identities can coexist.

qa.q: Sending aid to people affected by a disaster in another country reflects
qa.a: global solidarity
qa.e: It expresses cross-border concern.

qa.q: Which right is especially helped by global citizenship thinking?
qa.a: Protection of migrants and refugees across borders
qa.e: Global thinking protects people beyond borders.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Global citizenship is gaining importance. Reason (R): T.H. Marshall described citizenship in terms of civil, political and social rights.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true, but Marshall's categories do not explain the rise of global citizenship; border-crossing problems like climate change do.

qa.q: Which statement about global citizenship is most accurate?
qa.a: It encourages cross-border solidarity, though national citizenship still provides most rights
qa.e: A balanced view.

qa.q: Which is an example of nationalism as a unifying force?
qa.a: Unification of Italy in the 19th century
qa.e: Small states were united into one nation-state.

qa.q: Nationalism contributed to the break-up of which empires?
qa.a: The Austro-Hungarian and Ottoman empires
qa.e: These broke up in the early 20th century.

qa.q: India's freedom struggle is an example of nationalism
qa.a: inspiring a struggle against colonial rule
qa.e: Anti-colonial nationalism sought freedom.

qa.q: Nationalism can be divisive when
qa.a: groups claim exclusive belonging and turn against others
qa.e: Exclusive claims breed conflict.

qa.q: Which statement best sums up nationalism's role in history?
qa.a: It has both united peoples and caused conflicts
qa.e: Nationalism is double-edged.

qa.q: In the 19th century, German unification was driven largely by
qa.a: nationalism
qa.e: Nationalism unified German states.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Nationalism has been described as a double-edged force. Reason (R): It has inspired freedom struggles but also led to conflicts and hostility.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; its two contrasting effects are why it is double-edged.

qa.q: Separatist movements demanding a new state out of an existing one show nationalism as
qa.a: a force that can divide existing states
qa.e: Separatism divides states.

qa.q: Why is a nation called an 'imagined community'?
qa.a: It is held together by shared beliefs and imaginations of members who mostly never meet
qa.e: Shared imagination binds members.

qa.q: Which is NOT a necessary feature of a nation according to political theory?
qa.a: A single shared religion
qa.e: Nations can include many religions.

qa.q: Attachment to a particular homeland is the feature of
qa.a: territory
qa.e: Territory concerns the homeland.

qa.q: A sense of continuing historical identity in a nation is shown through
qa.a: shared memories, legends and historical records
qa.e: History binds members over time.

qa.q: Shared political ideals that can bind a nation include
qa.a: democracy, secularism and liberty
qa.e: Political values unite diverse people.

qa.q: Which statement about nations is correct?
qa.a: A nation exists to a large extent because its members believe it exists
qa.e: Shared belief is central.

qa.q: Assertion (A): India can be a nation despite great diversity. Reason (R): A nation can be based on shared political ideals and identity rather than one religion or language.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; shared ideals explain how a diverse India is a nation.

qa.q: Most members of a nation never meet one another. They still feel connected because of
qa.a: shared beliefs, history and political identity
qa.e: Common identity unites them.

qa.q: What is national self-determination?
qa.a: The claim of a nation to govern itself and have its own state
qa.e: It is a nation's claim to self-rule.

qa.q: After which event was the principle of 'one culture, one state' widely applied in Europe?
qa.a: The First World War
qa.e: Borders were redrawn after 1918.

qa.q: What was a major problem with 'one culture, one state'?
qa.a: Borders could not match mixed populations, creating new minorities and conflict
qa.e: Mixed populations made it impossible.

qa.q: Why does insisting on a separate state for every culture lead to conflict?
qa.a: Almost every state contains several cultural groups
qa.e: Endless division would follow.

qa.q: What alternative to creating new states for every group is suggested?
qa.a: Accommodating minorities within existing states by protecting their rights
qa.e: Accommodation is the preferred approach.

qa.q: Massive movements of people after redrawing borders show that
qa.a: self-determination can cause great human suffering if handled badly
qa.e: Forced migrations caused suffering.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Redrawing borders on cultural lines often created new minorities. Reason (R): Different cultural groups lived intermixed across regions.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; intermixed populations are why new minorities were created.

qa.q: Which approach does political theory generally favour for dealing with diverse groups within a state?
qa.a: Protecting minority rights and identities within the state
qa.e: Accommodation reduces conflict.

qa.q: What is pluralism?
qa.a: Recognising and respecting the diversity of groups within a nation
qa.e: Pluralism values diversity.

qa.q: Rabindranath Tagore's view of nationalism was that
qa.a: patriotism should not be placed above humanity
qa.e: He criticised narrow nationalism.

qa.q: Which is an example of India's pluralist approach?
qa.a: Protecting minorities' right to run educational institutions
qa.e: Minority rights reflect pluralism.

qa.q: Democratic nations recognise minority rights because
qa.a: minorities need protection of their language, culture and religion to be equal citizens
qa.e: Equality requires protecting minorities.

qa.q: Reorganising States on linguistic lines reflects
qa.a: accommodation of linguistic diversity
qa.e: Linguistic States recognise diversity.

qa.q: Tagore opposed colonial rule but also
qa.a: criticised narrow, aggressive nationalism
qa.e: He opposed both colonialism and narrow nationalism.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Pluralist nationalism can strengthen a diverse nation. Reason (R): When groups feel their identities are respected, they are more likely to feel part of the nation.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; respect for identities is how pluralism strengthens unity.

qa.q: Which feature would most likely be identified in a case study of a nation?
qa.a: Shared beliefs and political ideals among its members
qa.e: Shared beliefs and ideals mark a nation.

qa.q: Secularism is first and foremost a doctrine that
qa.a: opposes all forms of religious domination
qa.e: It targets domination, not religion.

qa.q: Inter-religious domination means
qa.a: one religious community dominating another
qa.e: 'Inter' means between religions.

qa.q: Which is an example of intra-religious domination?
qa.a: Discrimination by caste within the same religion
qa.e: Intra means within one religion.

qa.q: Why is secularism called a normative doctrine?
qa.a: It sets out an ideal of a society free from religious domination
qa.e: Normative means it prescribes ideals.

qa.q: Denying women equal rights within their own religious community is
qa.a: intra-religious domination
qa.e: It is domination within a religion.

qa.q: Secularism promotes
qa.a: freedom within religions and equality between and within them
qa.e: Freedom and equality are its aims.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Secularism addresses caste discrimination within a religion. Reason (R): Secularism opposes intra-religious as well as inter-religious domination.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; its opposition to intra-religious domination is why it addresses caste discrimination.

qa.q: Which statement about secularism is correct?
qa.a: It is compatible with people practising their religions freely
qa.e: It protects religious freedom while opposing domination.

qa.q: Which of the following is a feature of a secular state?
qa.a: It does not establish any official religion
qa.e: No state religion is basic to secularism.

qa.q: A state governed by religious leaders is called a
qa.a: theocratic state
qa.e: Theocracy is rule by religious heads.

qa.q: Why is separation of religion and state not enough for a state to be secular?
qa.a: The state must also be committed to freedom and equality for all religious groups
qa.e: Commitment to values is also needed.

qa.q: Which goal must a secular state promote?
qa.a: Equality between and within religions
qa.e: Equality is a core goal.

qa.q: A state with no official religion that still denies jobs to a religious minority is
qa.a: not truly secular
qa.e: Discrimination violates secular principles.

qa.q: In a secular state, religious institutions and state institutions are
qa.a: kept separate
qa.e: Institutional separation is a key feature.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A secular state must have an official religion that it treats with special respect. Reason (R): In a secular state, religious institutions and state institutions are kept separate.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: a secular state has no official religion. R is true.

qa.q: Which combination best describes a secular state?
qa.a: Separation from religious institutions plus commitment to peace, freedom and equality
qa.e: Both parts are needed.

qa.q: The Western model of secularism is based on
qa.a: mutual exclusion of state and religion
qa.e: Each keeps out of the other's sphere.

qa.q: Which is a feature of Indian secularism?
qa.a: It addresses both inter- and intra-religious domination
qa.e: It deals with domination at both levels.

qa.q: 'Principled distance' means that the state
qa.a: keeps a distance from religion but may intervene or support it to promote freedom and equality
qa.e: Engagement is guided by principles.

qa.q: Which is an example of state-led religious reform in India?
qa.a: Abolition of untouchability
qa.e: The state intervened to end discrimination.

qa.q: The Western model gives little attention to
qa.a: community-based rights of minorities
qa.e: It focuses on individuals.

qa.q: Allowing minorities to run educational institutions shows that Indian secularism
qa.a: recognises community rights as well as individual rights
qa.e: Community rights are part of the Indian model.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The Indian state can intervene in religious practices. Reason (R): Indian secularism is based on principled distance, which permits intervention to promote equality.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; principled distance is why intervention is allowed.

qa.q: Laws opening temples to people of all castes reflect
qa.a: the Indian model's concern with intra-religious equality
qa.e: Ending intra-religious domination is part of the Indian model.

qa.q: Which is a criticism of Indian secularism?
qa.a: It is a Western import alien to Indian culture
qa.e: Critics claim it is alien.

qa.q: The reply to the charge that secularism is anti-religious is that
qa.a: it opposes religious domination, not religion, and protects religious freedom
qa.e: Secularism protects freedom of religion.

qa.q: The criticism of 'minoritism' says that secularism
qa.a: favours minorities
qa.e: Critics allege favouritism.

qa.q: How do defenders respond to the 'interventionist' criticism?
qa.a: Intervention is meant to end discrimination such as untouchability, guided by principled distance
qa.e: Intervention has a purpose: equality.

qa.q: The 'vote-bank politics' criticism claims that
qa.a: secularism is used by parties to win the votes of particular groups
qa.e: It targets electoral misuse.

qa.q: Which criticism says secularism is too ambitious to be achieved?
qa.a: Impossible project
qa.e: It doubts the feasibility of the ideal.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Indian secularism has been called a 'Western import'. Reason (R): Indian secularism is identical to the Western model of strict separation.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false: Indian secularism differs from the Western model, with principled distance and community rights.

qa.q: A defender says minority rights in education protect basic interests of vulnerable groups. Which criticism is she answering?
qa.a: Minoritism
qa.e: The reply targets the claim of favouring minorities.
